Osteoblasts and osteoclasts are bone-remodeling cells that respond to the inflammatory milieu at the enthesis, but they are not located in the intestinal submucosa to trigger the initial IL-23 release.
While eosinophils are prominent in Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, they are not the primary cells responsible for IL-23 production in the pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis.
Chondrocytes and synovial fibroblasts are joint-resident cells involved in cartilage maintenance and matrix degradation; they do not participate in the primary mucosal immune trigger.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 975 (Book Page): In genetically susceptible individuals, it is thought that bacterial components penetrate the mucosal barrier to activate macrophages and dendritic cells in the intestinal submucosa. These cells produce increased amounts of interleukin (IL)-23.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of lower back pain that is most severe in the early morning and improves after a warm shower and exercise. Which of the following genetic markers is most strongly associated with this clinical presentation?
options: HLA-B51
HLA-DQ8
HLA-DR4
HLA-B27
HLA-DR3
correctOption: HLA-B27
optionExplanations: HLA-B51 is the hallmark genetic association for Behçet’s disease, which presents with oral/genital ulcers and uveitis, rather than primary axial spondyloarthritis.
HLA-DQ8 is associated with celiac disease and Type 1 diabetes mellitus, having no primary association with the pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis.
HLA-DR4 is primarily associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and is involved in the 'shared epitope' hypothesis, not ankylosing spondylitis.

HLA-B27 is a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecule strongly associated with axial spondyloarthritis, present in >95% of AS patients. It plays a role in antigen presentation and potentially the unfolded protein response triggering inflammation.
HLA-DR3 is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and Sjögren’s syndrome, typically involved in autoantibody-mediated connective tissue diseases.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): For AS there is a male-to-female ratio of about 3 : 1. In Europe, more than 90% of those affected are HLA-B27-positive (HLA-B27 population prevalence in those of European origin is 9%). The overall prevalence of AS is below 0.5% in most populations.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In the clinical assessment of axial spondyloarthritis, which pathophysiological mechanism best explains why patients experience relief of symptoms with physical activity rather than rest?
options: Downregulation of RANKL expression in subchondral bone
Passive stretching of the shortened longitudinal ligaments
Inhibition of the Th17 pathway by exercise-induced endorphins
Reduction of synovial fluid viscosity through mechanical shearing
Mechanical dispersal of inflammatory cytokines and improved blood flow
correctOption: Mechanical dispersal of inflammatory cytokines and improved blood flow
optionExplanations: RANKL is involved in bone erosions, particularly in RA. While important in AS, its downregulation is not the primary immediate reason for relief during a single exercise session.
Stretching may help flexibility but does not address the underlying cytokine-mediated stiffness that resolves with movement-induced circulation.
Endorphins provide analgesia but do not specifically target the IL-23/IL-17 inflammatory axis responsible for AS symptoms.
While synovial fluid viscosity changes in osteoarthritis, the primary relief in AS is due to the inflammatory nature of the disease where activity modulates cytokine levels.

Inflammatory back pain is characterized by the accumulation of inflammatory mediators during rest. Physical activity improves microcirculation and aids the clearance of these mediators from entheses and joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): The cardinal feature of axSpA is inflammatory back pain and early morning stiffness... Symptoms are exacerbated by inactivity and relieved by movement.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A patient diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis presents with a sudden onset of a painful, red, and photophobic right eye. Which extra-articular manifestation must be ruled out as the most common complication of this condition?
options: Episcleritis
Acute anterior uveitis
Scleritis
Retinal vasculitis
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
correctOption: Acute anterior uveitis
optionExplanations: Episcleritis is a benign, self-limiting inflammation of the episclera; while seen in various systemic diseases, it is not the 'cardinal' eye feature of AS.
Acute anterior uveitis (iritis) occurs in about 25-30% of AS patients. It presents with unilateral pain, redness, and photophobia, requiring urgent steroid treatment to prevent synechiae.
Scleritis is a more severe, sight-threatening inflammation of the sclera often associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis or GPA, but is less common in AS than uveitis.
Retinal vasculitis is an inflammation of the retinal vessels typically seen in Behçet’s disease or systemic vasculitides, but not usually in AS.
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye) is the hallmark of Sjögren’s syndrome and can be secondary to RA, but it is not the primary eye manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Acute anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature, which occasionally precedes joint disease.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 32-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain for 5 years. Physical examination reveals a Schober’s test result of 2 cm, chest expansion of 1.5 cm, and tenderness over the Achilles tendon insertion. Radiography reveals bilateral sacroiliitis. What is the most likely pathological driver for the new bone formation observed in this patient's condition?
options: IgG4-rich plasma cell infiltration of the vertebral endplates
IL-22 production by activated Th17 and other T cells
M-CSF mediated osteoclast recruitment at the joint margin
Matrix metalloproteinase-9 degradation of the annulus fibrosus
Autoantibody complexes targeting type II collagen
correctOption: IL-22 production by activated Th17 and other T cells
optionExplanations: IgG4-rich infiltration is characteristic of IgG4-related disease, a multi-organ fibro-inflammatory condition, not the standard pathology of ankylosing spondylitis.
While IL-17 drives inflammation and erosions, IL-22 (often co-produced by Th17 cells) specifically stimulates osteoblasts, leading to enthesitis-related ossification and syndesmophyte formation.
M-CSF is involved in osteoclastogenesis and bone erosion (destructive phase), whereas the hallmark of AS is osteoproliferation (new bone formation).
MMPs are involved in tissue destruction and cartilage breakdown, primarily seen in RA or erosive phases, but do not drive the 'bamboo spine' ossification.
AS is considered a seronegative spondyloarthropathy; it lacks autoantibodies like those targeting collagen, which are sometimes investigated in other arthritides.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in of axial spondyloarthritis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 40-year-old patient with ankylosing spondylitis reports severe pain at the heels when walking, especially during the first few steps in the morning. On examination, there is marked tenderness at the origin of the plantar fascia. This specific clinical feature is termed:
options: Enthesitis
Chondrocalcinosis
Synovitis
Bursitis
Dactylitis
correctOption: Enthesitis
optionExplanations: Enthesitis is the core pathological lesion in AS, involving inflammation at the insertion sites of tendons, ligaments, or joint capsules into bone, such as the plantar fascia or Achilles tendon.
Chondrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage, characteristic of pseudogout, not the inflammatory enthesopathy of AS.
Synovitis refers specifically to inflammation of the synovial lining of joints, whereas AS primarily targets the enthesis (where tendons/ligaments meet bone).
Bursitis is inflammation of the fluid-filled sacs (bursae) that cushion joints; while it can occur, it is not the primary pathological descriptor for the tendon-insertion pain in AS.
Dactylitis is 'sausage-like' swelling of an entire digit due to combined synovitis and tenosynovitis, common in Psoriatic Arthritis but not the specific term for tendon-to-bone insertion pain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone... typically affected include Achilles’ insertion, plantar fascia origin.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: According to the Assessment of Spondylitis International Society (ASAS) criteria, which of the following is required to classify a patient as having axial spondyloarthritis in the absence of radiographic sacroiliitis?
options: Bilateral Bouchard's nodes and morning stiffness > 1 hour
Positive Rheumatoid Factor and ESR > 50 mm/hr
Presence of HLA-B27 plus at least two other SpA features
Response to Methotrexate within 4 weeks
Presence of Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (ACP A) antibodies
correctOption: Presence of HLA-B27 plus at least two other SpA features
optionExplanations: Bouchard's nodes are characteristic of Osteoarthritis (PIP joints), not the axial inflammatory disease seen in AS.
AS is typically 'seronegative,' meaning Rheumatoid Factor is absent. High ESR is a feature but not a primary classification requirement.
The ASAS criteria allow for classification via the 'clinical arm' (HLA-B27 plus 2 features) or the 'imaging arm' (sacroiliitis on MRI/X-ray plus 1 feature).
Methotrexate is generally ineffective for the axial (spinal) symptoms of AS; response to NSAIDs, however, is a recognized SpA feature.
Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for Rheumatoid Arthritis and are typically negative in patients with ankylosing spondylitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis (ASAS)... In patients with > 3 months’ back pain and age at onset < 45 years... B: HLA-B27 plus ≥ 2 SpA features.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A patient with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis presents with a 'stooped' posture and an inability to look straight ahead. Which clinical measurement is most appropriate to quantify the severity of this spinal deformity?
options: Inter-incisor distance
Lateral lumbar flexion
Wrist circumference
Tragus-to-wall distance
Patellar tap test
correctOption: Tragus-to-wall distance
optionExplanations: Inter-incisor distance measures jaw opening, which can be affected in TMJ involvement but does not measure the spinal kyphotic stoop.
Lateral lumbar flexion measures the side-to-side mobility of the lower spine, which is reduced early in AS but is not the best measure for the forward-stooped (kyphotic) deformity.
Wrist circumference is irrelevant to the axial skeletal assessment and may be used in other contexts like growth or nutrition.
Tragus-to-wall distance measures the distance between the ear and the wall when a patient stands as straight as possible; it increases as cervical/thoracic kyphosis worsens.
The patellar tap test is used to identify a knee joint effusion, not to quantify spinal deformity or axial fusion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Spinal fusion can develop as AS progresses... a few patients develop marked kyphosis of the dorsal and cervical spine that may interfere with forward vision.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Fracture risk in an ankylosed spine
statement: A 45-year-old man with a 15-year history of ankylosing spondylitis experiences a sudden increase in localized back pain after a minor fall. Neurological exam is unremarkable. What is the most likely clinical complication necessitating urgent investigation in this patient?
options: Cauda equina syndrome due to disc herniation
Vertebral fracture
Secondary amyloidosis of the kidney
Acute aortic root dilatation
Spinal cord compression from a Baker's cyst
correctOption: Vertebral fracture
optionExplanations: While Cauda equina can occur in late AS due to chronic arachnoiditis, sudden localized pain after a fall in a fused spine most urgently suggests a fracture.
In AS, the fused 'bamboo spine' is rigid and osteoporotic, making it highly susceptible to fractures even with minor trauma. These fractures are often unstable and require immediate imaging.
Amyloidosis is a rare chronic complication of long-standing inflammation (AA amyloid) presenting with nephrotic syndrome, not acute spinal pain.
While aortic root lesions can occur in AS, they present with signs of aortic incompetence or conduction defects, not sudden localized back pain after trauma.
Baker's cysts occur in the popliteal fossa (knee) and do not cause spinal cord compression.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Osteoporosis is a common complication, particularly of the spine, leading to an increased risk of vertebral fracture.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: The development of 'bamboo spine' in ankylosing spondylitis is primarily the result of which continuous clinical process?
options: Calcification of the superficial layers of the articular cartilage
Degeneration of the intervertebral disc nucleus pulposus
Subchondral sclerosis of the facet joints alone
Hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum
Ossification of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus
correctOption: Ossification of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus
optionExplanations: Calcification of articular cartilage is 'chondrocalcinosis,' seen in CPPD, not the syndesmophyte formation characteristic of AS.
Disc degeneration is a feature of mechanical/degenerative spondylosis, whereas AS is characterized by inflammatory enthesopathy and subsequent ossification.
While facet joints do fuse in AS, the specific 'bamboo' radiographic appearance is created by the syndesmophytes along the vertebral bodies.
Ligamentum flavum hypertrophy is associated with spinal stenosis in osteoarthritis/degenerative disease, not the bridging ossification of AS.
Syndesmophytes are vertical bony bridges formed by the ossification of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus, which eventually join adjacent vertebrae to create the bamboo appearance.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Bridging syndesmophytes may also be seen. These are areas of calcification that follow the outermost fibres of the annulus (Fig. 26.41). In advanced disease... atypical ‘bamboo’ spine (Fig. 26.42).

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Pattern of joint involvement in SpA
statement: Which of the following describes the typical clinical distribution of peripheral arthritis when it occurs in patients with ankylosing spondylitis?
options: First metatarsophalangeal joint with extreme erythema
Asymmetrical involvement of large lower limb joints
Distal interphalangeal joints with nail pitting
Small joints of the hands in a symmetrical pattern
Proximal interphalangeal joints with Heberden's nodes
correctOption: Asymmetrical involvement of large lower limb joints
optionExplanations: First MTP involvement with extreme erythema is the hallmark of podagra in acute Gout.
When peripheral joints are involved in AS (and other SpAs), the pattern is typically an asymmetrical oligoarthritis (fewer than 5 joints) primarily affecting large joints like the hips or knees.
DIP joint involvement with nail changes is the classic presentation of Psoriatic Arthritis, though PsA is part of the SpA group, it is distinct from AS.
Symmetrical small joint involvement is the classic pattern of Rheumatoid Arthritis, not Spondyloarthritis.
PIP involvement with Heberden's nodes (actually DIP for Heberden's) describes nodal Osteoarthritis, not an inflammatory spondyloarthropathy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): In contrast to RA, in SpAs there are frequent and notable non-synovial musculoskeletal lesions... Page 1036 (Book Page): The onset is typically acute, with an inflammatory enthesitis, oligoarthritis... Lower limb joints and entheses are predominantly affected.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In the genetic evaluation of a patient suspected of having radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis), which percentage of patients typically tests positive for the HLA-B27 allele in European populations?
optionExplanations: In ankylosing spondylitis (AS), there is an exceptionally strong genetic association with HLA-B27, with more than 95% of patients carrying the allele.
50% is the frequency of certain manifestations in spondyloarthritis, such as subclinical inflammatory bowel disease, but not the genetic frequency of B27.
70% is the typical prevalence of Rheumatoid Factor and Anti-CCP in Rheumatoid Arthritis, not the prevalence of HLA-B27 in AS.
9% represents the background prevalence of HLA-B27 in the general European population, which is significantly lower than the rate in AS patients.
20% is the approximate frequency of HLA-B27 in patients with Psoriatic Arthritis of European descent.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): There is a striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which specific protein is implicated in the genetic predisposition to ankylosing spondylitis due to its role in facilitating intracellular antigen processing and binding with the MHC molecule HLA-B27?
options: ERAP-1
RANKL
ADAMTS-5
C1q complement
Matrix metalloproteinase
correctOption: ERAP-1
optionExplanations: ERAP-1 is an endoplasmic reticulum protein that trims peptides for presentation by MHC Class I molecules like HLA-B27; variants in this gene are major risk factors for AS.
RANKL is involved in osteoclast activation and bone erosion, primarily mentioned in the context of Rheumatoid Arthritis pathogenesis.
ADAMTS-5 is an aggrecanase involved in cartilage breakdown in osteoarthritis and RA, but is not the primary antigen processor for HLA-B27.
Inherited deficiencies in C1q are associated with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) due to defective apoptotic cell clearance, not AS.
Matrix metalloproteinases are enzymes that degrade cartilage and soft tissue, acting downstream of inflammatory cascades rather than as genetic processing precursors.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Other susceptibility genes also implicated in susceptibility to AS include ERAP-1 (an endoplasmic reticulum protein with a role facilitating intracellular antigen processing and binding with its presenting MHC molecule HLA-B27)

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: IL-17 and IL-22 Functional Contrast in AxSpA
statement: According to the current immunopathogenic model of axial spondyloarthritis, which statement best contrasts the roles of interleukin-17 (IL-17) and interleukin-22 (IL-22) in tissue damage?
options: IL-17 acts exclusively on the axial skeleton while IL-22 acts only on peripheral joints.
IL-17 inhibits osteoclast activity while IL-22 promotes chondrocyte apoptosis.
IL-17 is produced by dendritic cells and IL-22 is produced by macrophages to activate Th17 cells.
IL-17 has a pivotal role in driving inflammation and enthesitis while IL-22 is involved in causing new bone formation.
IL-17 is primarily responsible for new bone formation whereas IL-22 drives synovial hypertrophy.
correctOption: IL-17 has a pivotal role in driving inflammation and enthesitis while IL-22 is involved in causing new bone formation.
optionExplanations: Both cytokines are involved in the pathophysiology of spondyloarthritis generally, and their actions are not strictly restricted by anatomical location in the text's model.
The text does not state that IL-17 inhibits osteoclasts; rather, IL-17 is a key driver of inflammation and tissue destruction in AxSpA.
IL-23 is the cytokine produced by dendritic cells/macrophages that activates Th17 cells; IL-17 and IL-22 are products of the activated T cells themselves.
IL-17 is the central cytokine for inflammatory lesions (sacroiliitis/enthesitis), whereas IL-22 is implicated in the osteoproliferative aspect (syndesmophytes/ankylosis).
The text explicitly links IL-22 to new bone formation (syndesmophytes), not IL-17, which is the primary inflammatory mediator.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): IL-17 has a pivotal role in driving inflammation, causing sacroiliitis and enthesitis. Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in of axial spondyloarthritis.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 26-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of lower back pain that is worst in the early morning and improves with activity. He mentions a previous episode of painful red eye (uveitis). Physical examination reveals reduced lumbar spine flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. HLA-B27 testing is positive. Which pathophysiological mechanism involving the HLA-B27 molecule is most likely contributing to his condition's inflammatory trigger?
options: Binding of the molecule to the rheumatoid factor IgM complex.
Increased production of IL-10 by leukocytes activated by B27 monomers.
Deficiency in the molecule's ability to present viral antigens to CD4+ T cells.
Selective destruction of the vasa nervorum by B27-activated neutrophils.
Misfolding of the molecule causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress and cytokine release.
correctOption: Misfolding of the molecule causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress and cytokine release.
optionExplanations: Rheumatoid factor is typically absent in axial spondyloarthritis; this condition is a 'seronegative' spondyloarthropathy.
IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine; the pathogenesis of AS involves an increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-23 and IL-17.
HLA-B27 is an MHC Class I molecule and presents antigens to CD8+ T cells, not CD4+ T cells; furthermore, the pathogenesis involves an aberrant response, not a simple deficiency.
Destruction of the vasa nervorum is characteristic of Polyarteritis Nodosa, not the pathophysiology described for ankylosing spondylitis in the text.
The 'misfolding' hypothesis suggests that B27 molecules accumulate in the ER, triggering a stress response that results in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-23.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): HLA-B27 molecules may also misfold, causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress. This could lead to inflammatory cytokine release by macrophages and dendritic cells, thus triggering inflammatory disease.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In patients with axial spondyloarthritis who have an inadequate response to NSAIDs, biological therapy targeting which cytokine axis is indicated based on the disease's immunopathogenesis?
options: Interleukin-1 receptor antagonism
B-cell depletion via CD20 targeting
Interleukin-17A or IL-17A/F inhibition
Inhibition of IL-12 alone
Neutralization of nerve growth factor
correctOption: Interleukin-17A or IL-17A/F inhibition
optionExplanations: IL-1 inhibitors like anakinra are primarily used for Still’s disease and gout, but have little efficacy in ankylosing spondylitis.
B-cell depletion (Rituximab) is used in RA and SLE, but is not a standard or indicated treatment for axial spondyloarthritis according to the text.
Because the IL-23/IL-17 axis is central to the pathogenesis of AS, inhibitors of IL-17A (like secukinumab) are effective and indicated therapies.
While IL-12 and IL-23 share a subunit (p40), the specific Th17-driving cytokine in AS is IL-23; specific IL-17 inhibitors are the standard for AxSpA.
Nerve growth factor antibodies are under investigation for osteoarthritis pain but are not used to treat the underlying inflammation in AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1014 (Book Page): IL-17A and IL-17A/F. These drugs are indicated in adults with PsA and axSpA who have not responded adequately to cDMARDs and/or anti-TNF-α.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: According to the ASAS (Assessment of Spondylitis International Society) classification criteria, a diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis can be made in a patient with over 3 months of back pain and age of onset under 45 years if they possess which of the following?
options: Sacroiliitis on imaging plus at least one SpA feature.
ANA positivity plus malar rash and arthritis.
Positive Schirmer test and oral ulcers.
Positive RF and Anti-CCP with high ESR.
Symmetrical small joint arthritis and HLA-B27.
correctOption: Sacroiliitis on imaging plus at least one SpA feature.
optionExplanations: The ASAS criteria allow for diagnosis via two arms: the 'imaging arm' (Sacroiliitis + 1 feature) or the 'clinical arm' (HLA-B27 + 2 features).
These are criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), not axial spondyloarthritis.
A positive Schirmer test is used to diagnose Sjögren syndrome, and oral ulcers are typical of Behçet’s disease or SLE.
RF and Anti-CCP are markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis; axial spondyloarthritis is typically seronegative.
Axial spondyloarthritis typically involves asymmetrical oligoarthritis of the lower limbs, not symmetrical small joint arthritis (which is characteristic of RA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis (ASAS)... A: Sacroiliitis on imaging plus ≥ 1 SpA feature. B: HLA-B27 plus ≥ 2 SpA features.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: The immunopathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis suggests that the disease may be triggered by an interaction with the intestinal microbiota. Which specific organism's increased faecal carriage has been linked to exacerbations of both joint and eye disease in these patients?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Klebsiella aerogenes
Staphylococcus aureus
Hepatitis C virus
Borrelia burgdorferi
correctOption: Klebsiella aerogenes
optionExplanations: Chlamydia trachomatis is a common trigger for reactive arthritis, but the text specifically mentions Klebsiella in the context of AS exacerbations.
The text highlights Klebsiella aerogenes as a potential environmental trigger linked to the flares of AS and uveitis through mucosal immunity pathways.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis but is not specifically linked to the chronic gut-joint axis in AS.
Hepatitis C is associated with cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis and potentially viral arthritis, but not with the pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis.
Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of Lyme disease, which can cause late-stage arthritis but is not the trigger for AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Increased faecal carriage of Klebsiella aerogenes has been reported in patients with AS and may relate to exacerbation of both joint and eye disease.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Genetic Differentiation of PsA and AS
statement: A patient presents with musculoskeletal symptoms suggestive of a spondyloarthropathy. While Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is almost exclusively associated with HLA-B27, which genetic variant is specifically highlighted as a strong risk factor for Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA), distinguishing its genetic predisposition from pure AS?
options: IL-23 Receptor
HLA-DRB1
HLA-C
ERAP-1
STAT3
correctOption: HLA-C
optionExplanations: The IL-23 receptor is a common susceptibility gene across the spondyloarthritis spectrum and does not provide the specific genetic contrast offered by HLA-C markers.
HLA-DRB1 variants are the strongest associations for Rheumatoid Arthritis and Giant Cell Arteritis, not the primary MHC Class I risk for PsA.
While both AS and PsA share HLA-B27, PsA has an additional strong and specific association with HLA-C variants, which helps differentiate its genetic profile.
ERAP-1 is a key risk factor for AS, but its association with PsA is less central than the primary HLA-C and HLA-B variants mentioned.
STAT3 is a downstream signaling molecule involved in Th17 responses and is associated with AS, but it is not a primary MHC variant that distinguishes PsA from AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1037 (Book Page): Variants in the HLA-B and HLA-C genes are the strongest genetic risk factors [for PsA]... CD8+ T cells (which recognise antigen presented in the context of HLA class I) are more abundant than CD4+ T cells within the joint, which is in keeping with the genetic association between PsA and HLA-C and B variants.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which of the following describes the correctly sequence of the Th17 lymphocyte activation loop in the pathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis as described in the text?
options: C1q deficiency -> Apoptotic cell accumulation -> Polyclonal T-cell activation.
TNF-α activation -> B-cell proliferation -> IL-17 production.
HLA-B27 homodimers -> Neutrophil chemotaxis -> IL-1 production.
Microbial products -> Dendritic cell activation -> Increased IL-23 -> Th17 cell activation.
IL-22 release -> Osteoblast suppression -> RANKL production.
correctOption: Microbial products -> Dendritic cell activation -> Increased IL-23 -> Th17 cell activation.
optionExplanations: This loop describes the pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), not axial spondyloarthritis.
In AS, the primary driver is the IL-23/Th17 axis, not a primary TNF-α/B-cell loop as seen in other conditions.
While HLA-B27 homodimers play a role, the primary cytokine loop highlighted for Th17 activation in AS is mediated by IL-23.
The pathogenic loop begins with gut-related microbial products stimulating innate cells to produce IL-23, which then polarizes and activates Th17 cells.
IL-22 is involved in promoting new bone formation, not suppressing osteoblasts, and RANKL is usually associated with bone erosion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Additionally, SpAs are thought to arise as the result of an aberrant host response to infection and abnormal mucosal immunity primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In the context of the spondyloarthritides, what is the 'hallmark lesion' that occurs at the site where a ligament or tendon inserts into bone?
options: Pannus
Enthesitis
Subchondral sclerosis
Fibrinoid necrosis
Synovitis
correctOption: Enthesitis
optionExplanations: Pannus is the inflammatory synovial tissue characteristic of Rheumatoid Arthritis, which invades bone and cartilage.
Enthesitis is the definitive hallmark of SpAs (including AS and PsA), differentiating them from purely synovial diseases like RA.
Subchondral sclerosis is a radiographic feature of osteoarthritis, representing thickened bone under the cartilage.
Fibrinoid necrosis is a histological feature of vasculitis, involving the destruction of vessel walls.
Synovitis is general joint inflammation common in many arthritides; enthesitis is the more specific marker for the spondyloarthritis group.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Inflammatory vs Mechanical Back Pain Characteristics
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of lower back pain. Which of the following cardinal features would most strongly support a diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis over mechanical back pain?
options: Pain that is strictly localized to the lumbar vertebrae without radiation
Improvement of pain with movement and exacerbation with inactivity
Pain that is exacerbated by physical activity and relieved by bed rest
Sudden onset of sharp, radiating pain after lifting a heavy weight
Morning stiffness lasting less than 15 minutes that improves quickly
correctOption: Improvement of pain with movement and exacerbation with inactivity
optionExplanations: Axial spondyloarthritis pain frequently radiates to the buttocks or posterior thighs due to involvement of the sacroiliac joints, unlike localized mechanical muscular strain.
The classic inflammatory pattern of axial spondyloarthritis involves pain and stiffness that worsen during rest or inactivity and show marked improvement with exercise or movement.
Pain exacerbated by activity and relieved by rest is the hallmark of mechanical or degenerative spinal disease, such as osteoarthritis, rather than inflammatory spondyloarthritis.
Sudden onset of sharp pain following heavy lifting is characteristic of an acute disc herniation or mechanical strain, not the insidious onset typical of ankylosing spondylitis.
Morning stiffness in ankylosing spondylitis typically lasts significantly longer than 15 minutes; short-lived stiffness is more common in non-inflammatory conditions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): The cardinal feature of axSpA is inflammatory back pain and early morning stiffness... Symptoms are exacerbated by inactivity and relieved by movement.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In the pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis, which immunological pathway is primarily responsible for the activation of Th17 lymphocytes leading to the production of IL-17 and TNF-alpha?
options: Modification of host proteins through citrullination in the synovium
Direct invasion of the joint margin by proliferative pannus tissue
Deposition of basic calcium phosphate crystals in the fibrocartilage
Increased production of IL-23 in response to abnormal mucosal immunity
Activation of the RANKL pathway by synovial fibroblasts alone
correctOption: Increased production of IL-23 in response to abnormal mucosal immunity
optionExplanations: Citrullination is a key process in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis, leading to anti-CCP antibodies, but is not the primary driver in ankylosing spondylitis.
Pannus formation and direct invasion are characteristic of the erosive process in rheumatoid arthritis, whereas AS is characterized more by enthesitis and new bone formation.
Basic calcium phosphate deposition is associated with osteoarthritis and specific crystal-induced arthritides, not the primary inflammatory mechanism of AS-related sacroiliitis.
The IL-23/IL-17 axis is central to AS; IL-23 production, likely triggered by gut mucosal dysbiosis, stimulates Th17 cells to release pro-inflammatory IL-17 and TNF-alpha.
While RANKL is involved in osteoclast activation in many inflammatory states, it is a downstream effector rather than the primary immune trigger in the AS IL-23/Th17 pathway.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): SpAs are thought to arise as the result of an aberrant host response to infection and abnormal mucosal immunity primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Enthesitis as a Hallmark of SpA
statement: When differentiating axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) from other causes of chronic back pain, which clinical finding is considered a hallmark lesion of the spondyloarthritides?
options: Symmetrical involvement of the small joints of the hands
Enthesitis, such as inflammation at the Achilles tendon insertion
Tophi on the extensor surfaces of the forearms
Heberden's nodes at the distal interphalangeal joints
Subchondral sclerosis and osteophyte formation on X-ray
correctOption: Enthesitis, such as inflammation at the Achilles tendon insertion
optionExplanations: Symmetrical small joint involvement is the classic presentation of rheumatoid arthritis, whereas AS typically targets the axial skeleton and large lower limb joints asymmetrically.
Enthesitis, inflammation where tendons or ligaments attach to bone (like the Achilles tendon or plantar fascia), is the definitive pathological feature of the spondyloarthritis group.
Tophi are deposits of monosodium urate crystals characteristic of chronic gout, not the inflammatory or ossifying lesions found in ankylosing spondylitis.
Heberden's nodes are characteristic of nodal osteoarthritis and represent bony overgrowth at the DIP joints, not the inflammatory enthesitis seen in AS.
Subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes are the primary radiological features of osteoarthritis, representing degenerative repair, distinct from the syndesmophytes seen in AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 32-year-old male presents with chronic low back pain for 2 years and a history of painful red eye treated as uveitis. Physical exam shows reduced lumbar spine flexion in all directions and pain on sacroiliac stressing. Lab tests show positive HLA-B27 and an ESR of 55 mm/hr. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm 'Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis'?
options: Plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints to identify erosions, sclerosis, or fusion
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest to screen for apical pulmonary fibrosis
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine to detect bone marrow oedema
Serum uric acid levels to rule out axial crystal deposition
Synovial fluid analysis of the knee to look for Th17 lymphocyte counts
correctOption: Plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints to identify erosions, sclerosis, or fusion
optionExplanations: Radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis) is defined by visible structural changes on plain X-rays, including sacroiliac joint narrowing, sclerosis, or ankylosis.
While upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis is a rare extra-articular feature of AS, it is not a diagnostic criterion for the musculoskeletal involvement of the disease.
MRI is highly sensitive for 'Non-radiographic axSpA' by detecting bone marrow oedema, but the diagnosis of AS specifically requires definitive changes visible on a plain X-ray.
Axial gout is rare and would not explain the combination of HLA-B27 positivity, uveitis, and chronic inflammatory back pain pattern typical of AS.
Synovial fluid analysis is not part of the standard diagnostic criteria for AS; diagnosis relies on clinical features and imaging of the axial skeleton.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): A diagnosis of AS (radiographic axSpA), which requires evidence of these radiographic changes on X-ray, may only be applied many years after a patient’s symptoms started.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Drug Selection in Comorbid AS and IBD
statement: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis is being considered for biologics. If this patient also has a comorbid diagnosis of Crohn's disease, which of the following pharmacological agents should be avoided due to the risk of triggering flares?
options: Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) inhibitors
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
Conventional DMARDs like Sulfasalazine
Interleukin-12/23 inhibitors
Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors
correctOption: Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) inhibitors
optionExplanations: IL-17A inhibitors, while highly effective for the skin and joints in SpA, are contraindicated in patients with inflammatory bowel disease as they can worsen or trigger IBD flares.
While NSAIDs can exacerbate IBD, the text specifically highlights the risk of anti-IL-17A therapy in triggering flares, whereas NSAIDs are the first-line treatment for AS symptoms.
Sulfasalazine is a conventional DMARD that can be used for the peripheral manifestations of both AS and IBD, though it does not improve the axial symptoms of AS.
IL-12/23 inhibitors (like ustekinumab) are used in IBD and psoriatic arthritis, though their role in pure axial AS is less established than TNF inhibitors.
TNF-alpha inhibitors are generally effective for both ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease, making them a suitable choice for this comorbid presentation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Anti-IL-17A therapy should be avoided as it can trigger flares of IBD.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: According to the ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis, what is the required age at onset and symptom duration for a patient to enter the classification pathway?
options: Age at onset < 40 years and duration > 1 year
Age at onset < 50 years and duration > 6 months
Age at onset > 60 years and duration > 1 month
Age at onset < 16 years and duration > 6 weeks
Age at onset < 45 years and duration > 3 months
correctOption: Age at onset < 45 years and duration > 3 months
optionExplanations: While many patients present under 40, the official threshold is 45, and waiting for 1 year of symptoms is not required for classification or diagnosis under modern guidelines.
The age cutoff is 45, not 50, and the duration requirement is 3 months, reflecting the chronic nature of inflammatory back pain.
Axial spondyloarthritis almost always presents before the age of 45; a new onset of back pain in a 60-year-old is much more likely to be degenerative or metastatic.
Age under 16 is the criterion for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis, and 6 weeks is the typical symptom duration used in rheumatoid arthritis criteria.
The ASAS criteria specifically target young adults (onset under 45 years) with chronic back pain (persisting for more than 3 months) to differentiate from common mechanical pain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Box 26.60 Classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis (ASAS). In patients with > 3 months’ back pain and age at onset < 45 years...

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Clinical and Radiological Progression of AS
statement: A patient with established ankylosing spondylitis presents for a routine check-up. Which physical finding would indicate advanced progression and fusion of the spinal column?
options: Presence of a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds
Loss of lumbar lordosis and the development of a 'bamboo' appearance on imaging
Increased lumbar lordosis and hypermobility of the neck
Crepitus and bony swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints
Symmetrical swelling and pitting oedema of the small joints of the feet
correctOption: Loss of lumbar lordosis and the development of a 'bamboo' appearance on imaging
optionExplanations: A malar rash is the classic feature of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and is not a feature of ankylosing spondylitis.
Progression of AS involves the ossification of spinal ligaments and the formation of bridging syndesmophytes, leading to a rigid 'bamboo spine' and loss of normal lumbar curvature.
AS typically leads to the loss of lumbar lordosis and a fixed stoop, rather than increased lordosis or hypermobility; fusion severely restricts all spinal movement.
Crepitus and DIP joint swelling are features of osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes), which targets different joints than the axial-predominant ankylosing spondylitis.
Pitting oedema and symmetrical small joint polyarthritis are more typical of acute onset rheumatoid arthritis or certain viral arthritides, not the chronic axial fusion of AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Spinal fusion can develop as AS progresses... Physical signs include a reduced range of lumbar spine movements in all directions... Page 1035 (Book Page): The combination of these features may result in the typical ‘bamboo’ spine.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 40-year-old male with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis presents with new-onset exertional breathlessness. Clinical examination reveals a diastolic murmur at the right second intercostal space. Which extra-articular feature of AS is most likely responsible?
options: Atypical upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis
Prostatitis with systemic inflammatory response
Secondary amyloidosis leading to restrictive cardiomyopathy
Aortic root disease leading to aortic incompetence
Interstitial nephritis causing fluid overload
correctOption: Aortic root disease leading to aortic incompetence
optionExplanations: Upper lobe fibrosis can occur in AS, but it causes pulmonary symptoms and would not explain a heart murmur indicative of aortic valve dysfunction.
Prostatitis is very common in men with AS (80%), but it typically causes local urogenital symptoms rather than cardiac murmurs or breathlessness.
While amyloidosis is a rare complication of chronic AS, the specific finding of a diastolic murmur points directly to valvular incompetence rather than cardiomyopathy.
Inflammation of the aortic root in AS patients can lead to aortic valve incompetence (present in up to 20%), which clinically presents as a diastolic murmur and potential heart failure.
Interstitial nephritis is more common in Sjögren syndrome or SLE; renal involvement in AS is typically limited to secondary amyloidosis or NSAID-related issues.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Extra-articular features of axial spondyloarthritis... Cardiovascular disease (aortic valve disease 20%).

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Cytokine Roles in AS: Inflammation vs Ossification
statement: In the physiological regulation of bone remodeling in axial spondyloarthritis, which cytokine is specifically implicated in the pathological 'new bone formation' that leads to syndesmophytes?
options: Interleukin-22 (IL-22)
Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ)
Interleukin-1 (IL-1)
Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNF)-alpha
Matrix Metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9)
correctOption: Interleukin-22 (IL-22)
optionExplanations: IL-22, produced by Th17 and other immune cells, stimulates osteoblasts and is specifically linked to the pathological ossification (syndesmophyte formation) characteristic of AS.
Interferon-gamma is primarily involved in macrophage activation and Th1 responses, contributing to the inflammatory state but not specifically the ossification process.
IL-1 is a key driver of acute inflammation and bone resorption in diseases like RA and gout, but is not the primary driver of the new bone formation in AS.
TNF-alpha is a major driver of the 'inflammation' in AS, but ironically, blocking TNF does not always stop the progression of new bone formation (syndesmophytes).
MMPs are enzymes that degrade the extracellular matrix and are involved in joint destruction and cartilage breakdown, rather than the formation of new bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Fig 26.39... Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in axial spondyloarthritis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which of the following extra-articular clinical features is noted to occur in as many as 80% of men diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis?
options: Psoriasis
Aortic incompetence
Prostatitis
Inflammatory bowel disease
Acute anterior uveitis
correctOption: Prostatitis
optionExplanations: Psoriasis is a common overlap in the spondyloarthritis group, but its prevalence in primary ankylosing spondylitis is much lower than 80%.
Aortic valve disease/incompetence occurs in about 20% of patients with long-standing disease, making it significant but far less common than prostatitis.
Prostatitis, often sterile, is remarkably common in men with AS, occurring in approximately 80% of cases according to standard rheumatology references.
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's/Colitis) is clinically apparent in about 5-10% and histologically present in up to 50%, but not 80%.
Acute anterior uveitis is the most common 'symptomatic' extra-articular feature, but it occurs in about 25% of patients, not 80%.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Box 26.61 Extra-articular features of axial spondyloarthritis... Prostatitis (80% of men) and sterile urethritis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with a 4-month history of insidious low back pain. According to the ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis, what is the maximum age at onset of back pain to be considered for this diagnosis?
options: 50 years
35 years
45 years
55 years
40 years
correctOption: 45 years
optionExplanations: 50 years is beyond the standard classification cutoff; patients presenting with first-onset inflammatory back pain at 50 are more likely to have other pathologies or do not meet the ASAS definition.
35 years is too young a threshold; while many patients present earlier, the official criteria allow for an older cut-off to capture later-onset axial spondyloarthritis cases.
According to the ASAS criteria, the onset of inflammatory back pain must occur before the age of 45 years in patients who have had symptoms for more than 3 months.
55 years is typical for degenerative disc disease or osteoarthritis rather than ankylosing spondylitis, which classically affects young adults before the fifth decade of life.
40 years is a common clinical suspicion age, but the formal ASAS classification criteria specifically use 45 years as the age limit for the onset of back pain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): In patients with > 3 months’ back pain and age at onset < 45 years, either A or B is present: A: Sacroiliitis on imaging plus ≥ 1 SpA feature B: HLA-B27 plus ≥ 2 SpA features

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: The pathogenesis of enthesitis and new bone formation in axial spondyloarthritis is primarily mediated by which specific immunological signaling pathway?
options: Complement C3/C4 activation via immune complex deposition
IL-4/IL-5 secretion by Th2 lymphocytes
IL-1/IL-6 axis via B-lymphocyte activation
IFN-gamma/TNF-alpha loop in synovial fibroblasts
IL-23/IL-17 axis causing Th17 cell activation
correctOption: IL-23/IL-17 axis causing Th17 cell activation
optionExplanations: Complement activation is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus and other immune-complex mediated vasculitides, but it does not drive the enthesitis in AS.
The Th2 pathway is associated with allergic responses and asthma; ankylosing spondylitis is a Th17-driven autoimmune/autoinflammatory condition.
IL-1 and IL-6 are prominent in Rheumatoid Arthritis and systemic JIA, but they are not the primary drivers of the enthesitis-specific pathology seen in ankylosing spondylitis.
While TNF-alpha is involved and targeted by drugs, the upstream driver is the IL-23/IL-17 axis; IFN-gamma is more characteristic of T-cell mediated granulomatous diseases.

The IL-23/IL-17 axis is the hallmark of SpA. IL-23 activates Th17 cells, leading to the production of IL-17 and IL-22, which promote both inflammation and the characteristic new bone formation (syndesmophytes).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): spondyloarthritides are thought to arise as the result of an aberrant host response to infection and abnormal mucosal immunity primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A patient describes his low back pain as being most severe during the early morning hours, often waking him up at 3:00 AM. He notes that the stiffness improves significantly after a hot shower and a brief walk. This pattern of 'inflammatory' back pain is best contrasted with 'mechanical' pain by which feature?
options: Improvement of symptoms with prolonged bed rest
Sudden onset of pain following heavy lifting
Relief of symptoms with movement and activity
Exacerbation of symptoms during physical exercise
Pain that is localized strictly to the mid-thoracic spine
correctOption: Relief of symptoms with movement and activity
optionExplanations: Mechanical pain often improves with rest; in contrast, rest or inactivity typically worsens the stiffness and pain of ankylosing spondylitis.
Sudden onset after lifting suggests a mechanical cause like an acute disc prolapse; AS usually has an insidious onset over several months.
The fundamental clinical distinction is that inflammatory back pain (like in AS) improves with activity and movement, while mechanical pain is aggravated by it.
Exacerbation with exercise is a hallmark of mechanical back pain, such as muscle strain or disc herniation, whereas AS pain improves with movement.
AS pain typically starts in the sacroiliac joints (buttock pain) or the lumbar region; thoracic pain can occur but is not the defining contrast for mechanical vs. inflammatory patterns.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): The cardinal feature of axSpA is inflammatory back pain and early morning stiffness... Symptoms are exacerbated by inactivity and relieved by movement.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 30-year-old male presents with chronic bilateral buttock pain, a red painful right eye with photophobia, and tenderness over the insertion of the Achilles tendon. Physical examination reveals a reduced range of lumbar movement in all planes. Which clinical finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (AS)?
options: Symmetrical involvement of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints
Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer of 1:160
Presence of rheumatoid nodules on the extensor surfaces
Elevated serum uric acid levels exceeding 8 mg/dL
Radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis
correctOption: Radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis
optionExplanations: DIP joint involvement is characteristic of Psoriatic Arthritis or Osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes), not the primary spinal presentation of AS.
ANA is a screening marker for SLE and other connective tissue diseases; it is not a feature of AS and would likely point toward a different diagnosis.
Rheumatoid nodules are characteristic of seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis and are generally absent in the spondyloarthritides.
Hyperuricaemia is the metabolic hallmark of gout; although gout can cause monoarthritis, it does not explain chronic axial stiffness and uveitis.
By definition, 'radiographic' axial spondyloarthritis (Ankylosing Spondylitis) requires the presence of sacroiliitis visible on X-ray according to the Modified New York criteria.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): A diagnosis of AS (radiographic axSpA), which requires evidence of these radiographic changes on X-ray, may only be applied many years after a patient’s symptoms started.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: In the management and clinical evaluation of a patient suspected of having ankylosing spondylitis, which pharmacological response is included as a supportive 'feature' in the ASAS classification criteria?
options: Rapid relief of symptoms with oral glucocorticoids
Significant clinical improvement with a 48-hour trial of NSAIDs
Reduction in joint swelling following a single dose of Allopurinol
Complete resolution of morning stiffness with Colchicine
Slowing of spinal fusion progression with Methotrexate
correctOption: Significant clinical improvement with a 48-hour trial of NSAIDs
optionExplanations: While glucocorticoids are used for uveitis or peripheral joints, they do not help spinal disease in AS and are not a classification feature.
A 'Good response to NSAIDs' is a recognized clinical feature in the ASAS criteria, as inflammatory back pain in AS typically responds very well to these agents.
Allopurinol is for gout prophylaxis and has no role in the diagnosis or treatment of axial spondyloarthritis.
Colchicine is primarily for gout or CPPD and does not target the spinal inflammation characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis.
Methotrexate is used for peripheral arthritis in AS but has been proven to have no impact on spinal symptoms or the progression of spinal fusion/ankylosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): SpA features are: ... Good response to NSAIDs

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: What is the approximate prevalence of the HLA-B27 genotype in patients of European descent specifically diagnosed with Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)?
optionExplanations: 50% is too low; HLA-B27 is much more tightly linked to AS than many other genetic markers are to their respective diseases.
While 85% is high, it still underestimates the association in AS, which is one of the strongest MHC-disease links in medicine.
70% is the prevalence of Rheumatoid Factor in RA, but the HLA-B27 association in AS is even stronger.
In patients with a confirmed diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis (radiographic axial SpA), the HLA-B27 genotype is found in more than 95% of cases in European populations.
20% is the approximate carriage rate of HLA-B27 in Psoriatic Arthritis, but it is significantly higher in AS.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): There is a striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: During a physical examination of a patient with suspected advanced ankylosing spondylitis, the clinician assesses spinal mobility. Which finding is most characteristic of the disease?
options: Isolated restriction of lumbar extension with preserved flexion
Reduced range of lumbar spine movements in all directions
Hypermobility of the interspinous ligaments
Increased lumbar lordosis with normal cervical mobility
Painful restriction of internal rotation of the hip only
correctOption: Reduced range of lumbar spine movements in all directions
optionExplanations: AS typically involves a global loss of movement (flexion, extension, and lateral rotation) rather than a loss in just one plane.
The inflammatory and subsequent fibrotic/bony changes in AS lead to a characteristic global reduction in spinal mobility in all directions (flexion, extension, and lateral bending).
AS causes ankylosis (fusion), which leads to extreme rigidity (stiffness), the opposite of hypermobility.
AS typically causes a 'loss' of lumbar lordosis and the development of dorsal kyphosis, rather than an increase in lordosis.
Restricted internal rotation of the hip is the earliest sign of hip osteoarthritis, not the primary spinal sign for AS, though AS can involve the hips later.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): Physical signs include a reduced range of lumbar spine movements in all directions, pain on sacroiliac stressing and a high enthesitis index.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 45-year-old patient with a 20-year history of ankylosing spondylitis presents with sudden-onset shortness of breath. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur at the right second intercostal space and bilateral apical crackles. Which extra-articular feature of AS is most likely responsible for these findings?
options: Secondary amyloidosis leading to nephrotic syndrome
Restrictive lung disease due to costovertebral ankylosis
Mitral valve prolapse and pulmonary hypertension
Pericardial effusion and pleural thickening
Aortic root lesions and upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis
correctOption: Aortic root lesions and upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis
optionExplanations: While amyloidosis is a rare complication of chronic AS, it typically presents as renal failure or nephrotic syndrome, not a cardiac murmur and lung crackles.
Costovertebral ankylosis causes restrictive lung disease, but this results in decreased chest expansion rather than localized apical crackles and heart murmurs.
Mitral valve prolapse is not the classic cardiac lesion in AS; rather, the aortic valve and aortic root are typically targeted.
Pericarditis can occur, but the specific combination of a diastolic murmur and apical lung findings specifically points to the aortic root and upper lobe fibrosis.
AS is associated with aortic root lesions (causing aortic incompetence/diastolic murmurs) and, rarely, atypical upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, which can explain the apical crackles.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Extra-articular features... Cardiovascular disease (aortic valve disease 20%)... Atypical upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis (very rare).

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which cytokine is specifically implicated in the pathological process of new bone formation (osteoproliferation) in axial spondyloarthritis, potentially distinguishing it from the purely erosive nature of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
options: IL-22
IL-10
IL-12
IL-2
TGF-beta
correctOption: IL-22
optionExplanations: IL-22, produced by Th17 and Th22 cells, is significantly involved in driving osteoblast activity and the formation of syndesmophytes in AS.
IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that generally inhibits immune responses; it does not drive the bone formation seen in AS.
IL-12 is involved in Th1 differentiation and the production of IFN-gamma, but it is not the primary driver of new bone formation in the SpA group.
IL-2 is primarily a T-cell growth factor; it does not directly regulate the bone remodeling or syndesmophyte formation in AS.
TGF-beta is a general factor in fibrosis and tissue repair, but IL-22 is the specific cytokine highlighted in the text as driving the AS-specific osteoproliferative process.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in of axial spondyloarthritis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which extra-articular clinical feature is recognized as the most common systemic manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis?
options: Secondary Amyloidosis
Acute Anterior Uveitis
Psoriatic Skin Plaques
Apical Pulmonary Fibrosis
Aortic Valve Insufficiency
correctOption: Acute Anterior Uveitis
optionExplanations: Amyloidosis is a rare, late complication of chronic inflammation in AS, occurring in a very small percentage of patients.
Acute anterior uveitis (iritis) occurs in about 25-30% of AS patients and is definitively the most common extra-articular manifestation.
Psoriasis can be part of the SpA spectrum, but it is a defining characteristic of Psoriatic Arthritis, not the 'most common' feature within idiopathic AS.
Upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis is documented in AS but is considered 'very rare' according to clinical literature.
Aortic valve disease occurs in about 20% of patients with long-standing AS, making it common but still less frequent than uveitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1033 (Book Page): Acute anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature, which occasionally precedes joint disease.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Epidemiological Gender Distribution of Ankylosing Spondylitis
statement: Which of the following is the most accurate male-to-female ratio observed in patients diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis)?
optionExplanations: A 1:3 ratio would suggest a female predominance, which is characteristic of Rheumatoid Arthritis, not ankylosing spondylitis.
A 1:1 ratio is incorrect as ankylosing spondylitis shows a distinct male predominance in clinical presentation and radiographic progression.
A 5:1 ratio is observed in gout prevalence, but exceeds the established ratio for axial spondyloarthritis.
Ankylosing spondylitis is significantly more common in males, with the established clinical ratio being approximately 3:1.
A 10:1 ratio is characteristic of the female predominance in fibromyalgia or systemic lupus erythematosus, not ankylosing spondylitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): For AS there is a male-to-female ratio of about 3: 1.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: The IL-23/IL-17 Immunological Axis in SpA
statement: In the pathophysiology of axial spondyloarthritis, which immunological pathway is primarily responsible for the activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17 and TNF-α?
options: RANK/RANKL pathway
IL-12/Th1 pathway
IL-23/Th17 axis
IL-1/IL-6 axis
IFN-γ/Macrophage loop
correctOption: IL-23/Th17 axis
optionExplanations: The RANK/RANKL pathway is primarily involved in osteoclast activation and bone erosion, rather than the initial activation of Th17 lymphocytes.
IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation; in SpA, the IL-23 (which shares a p40 subunit with IL-12) specifically drives the Th17 pathway.
Increased IL-23 production, often triggered by mucosal immunity issues, drives the expansion of Th17 cells, which are the primary source of the IL-17 that causes enthesitis and sacroiliitis.
While IL-1 and IL-6 are pro-inflammatory, the specific driver for Th17 differentiation in spondyloarthritis is IL-23.
The IFN-γ loop is more characteristic of Th1 responses and granuloma formation in conditions like sarcoidosis, though it plays minor roles in other inflammatory states.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): spondyloarthritides are thought to arise as the result of an aberrant host response to infection and abnormal mucosal immunity primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A patient presents with chronic low back pain. Which clinical characteristic most strongly suggests an inflammatory etiology such as ankylosing spondylitis rather than a mechanical cause?
options: Pain that is exacerbated by physical activity
Sudden onset following a heavy lifting episode
Pain that is most severe in the late evening
Improvement of symptoms with rest
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes that improves with exercise
correctOption: Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes that improves with exercise
optionExplanations: Pain exacerbated by activity is a hallmark of mechanical back pain or osteoarthritis, not inflammatory spondyloarthritis.
Sudden onset following trauma or lifting is typical of mechanical strains or disc herniations.
Mechanical pain often worsens throughout the day with use, whereas inflammatory pain is typically worst after periods of prolonged inactivity, such as sleep.
Rest typically improves mechanical pain but exacerbates the stiffness and pain associated with ankylosing spondylitis.
Inflammatory back pain is classically improved by movement and exercise and is associated with significant early morning stiffness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): The cardinal feature of axSpA is inflammatory back pain and early morning stiffness... Symptoms are exacerbated by inactivity and relieved by movement.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A 26-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of dull buttock pain that is worse at 4 AM and associated with 2 hours of morning stiffness. He has a history of painful red eye treated by an ophthalmologist last year. Pelvic MRI reveals bone marrow oedema around the sacroiliac joints. Based on the ASAS classification criteria, which finding would most definitively classify him as having axial spondyloarthritis?
options: Presence of Heberden's nodes
Response to acetaminophen
Positive HLA-B27 genotype
Elevated Rheumatoid Factor
Presence of subcutaneous nodules
correctOption: Positive HLA-B27 genotype
optionExplanations: Heberden's nodes are characteristic of nodal osteoarthritis of the DIP joints, not axial spondyloarthritis.
The criteria specify a 'good response to NSAIDs', not acetaminophen, which has minimal anti-inflammatory effect.

The patient meets the imaging arm (Sacroiliitis on MRI) and has SpA features (inflammatory back pain, history of uveitis). HLA-B27 is a core genetic marker that provides a definitive classification arm in the ASAS criteria.
Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy; Rheumatoid Factor is typically negative.
Subcutaneous nodules are a feature of Rheumatoid Arthritis, not the spondyloarthritides.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): In patients with > 3 months’ back pain and age at onset < 45 years, either A or B is present: A: Sacroiliitis on imaging plus ≥ 1 SpA feature B: HLA-B27 plus ≥ 2 SpA features

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Limitation of cDMARDs in Axial SpA
statement: Regarding the pharmacological management of axial spondyloarthritis, which statement correctly distinguishes the utility of conventional synthetic DMARDs (cDMARDs) in this condition?
options: cDMARDs like Sulfasalazine have no significant impact on spinal symptoms
Hydroxychloroquine is indicated for preventing syndesmophyte formation
Leflunomide is superior to TNF-α inhibitors for axial disease
Methotrexate is highly effective for reducing spinal stiffness and ankylosis
Sulfasalazine is the first-line treatment for axial spinal symptoms
correctOption: cDMARDs like Sulfasalazine have no significant impact on spinal symptoms
optionExplanations: Clinical evidence confirms that cDMARDs like Methotrexate and Sulfasalazine are effective for peripheral joints but fail to alleviate spinal symptoms or slow axial progression.
Hydroxychloroquine is generally not used in AS and has no role in preventing the ossification of spinal ligaments (syndesmophytes).
TNF-α inhibitors are the gold standard for cDMARD-resistant axial disease; Leflunomide does not have evidence for axial efficacy.
Methotrexate has not been shown to be effective for the axial (spinal) manifestations of AS.
Sulfasalazine is useful for peripheral arthritis in AS but is not recommended for treating purely axial disease.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): For severe and/or persistent peripheral joint involvement, both SSZ and MTX are reasonable therapy choices. These medications have no impact on spinal symptoms or disease progression.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: What is the most common extra-articular manifestation associated with ankylosing spondylitis, occurring in approximately 25% of patients?
options: Amyloidosis
Acute anterior uveitis
Aortic regurgitation
IgA nephropathy
Apical lung fibrosis
correctOption: Acute anterior uveitis
optionExplanations: Amyloidosis is a rare complication of chronic inflammatory states like long-standing AS.
Acute anterior uveitis is the hallmark extra-articular feature of AS, presenting with unilateral eye pain, redness, and photophobia.
Aortic valve disease occurs in approximately 20% of patients with long-standing disease, but uveitis is more frequent.
While IgA levels may be elevated, IgA nephropathy is not the primary common extra-articular clinical manifestation listed in the core statistics.
Upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis is a recognized feature but is considered very rare.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Acute anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature... Page 1035 (Book Page): Anterior uveitis (25%)

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: A patient with suspected ankylosing spondylitis is evaluated for enthesitis. Which of the following anatomical sites is most characteristically involved in the inflammatory enthesopathy of this condition?
options: Insertion of the sartorius on the tibia
Insertion of the Achilles tendon on the calcaneus
Origin of the brachioradialis
Bicipital groove of the humerus
Insertion of the deltoid on the humerus
correctOption: Insertion of the Achilles tendon on the calcaneus
optionExplanations: The Pes Anserinus (where sartorius inserts) can be involved in bursitis, but the Achilles insertion is the classic site described for SpA enthesitis.
Achilles tendonitis at the calcaneal insertion is a hallmark 'cardinal' feature of the spondyloarthritides.
The brachioradialis origin is not a standard site for the enthesitis index in AS.
Bicipital tendonitis is more commonly associated with mechanical shoulder impingement than with systemic enthesitis of AS.
While enthesitis can be widespread, the deltoid insertion is not among the classic high-yield sites like the Achilles or plantar fascia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1034 (Book Page): Entheses that are typically affected include Achilles’ insertion, plantar fascia origin, patellar ligament entheses, gluteus medius insertion at the greater trochanter and tendon attachments at humeral epicondyles.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
coreConcept: Radiographic Distinction Between AS and other SpAs
statement: A 32-year-old female with a history of Crohn’s disease develops inflammatory-type neck and low back pain. Radiographs of the spine show coarse, asymmetrical, non-marginal syndesmophytes and unilateral sacroiliitis. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
options: Psoriatic Spondylitis or Enteropathic SpA
Mechanical Lumbar Spondylosis
Osteoporotic vertebral fracture
Primary Ankylosing Spondylitis
Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH)
correctOption: Psoriatic Spondylitis or Enteropathic SpA
optionExplanations: Asymmetrical sacroiliitis and non-marginal (bulky) syndesmophytes are characteristic of psoriatic arthritis and the spondylitis associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
Mechanical spondylosis presents with osteophytes (bony spurs) rather than syndesmophytes, and does not involve sacroiliitis.
Vertebral fractures involve loss of vertebral height and do not present with syndesmophyte formation or sacroiliitis.
Primary AS typically presents with symmetrical sacroiliitis and marginal, fine syndesmophytes, unlike the coarse asymmetrical ones described.
DISH presents with flowing ossification over at least four contiguous vertebrae but typically spares the sacroiliac joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1037 (Book Page): In contrast to AS, radiographic sacroiliitis is often asymmetrical and sometimes unilateral, and syndesmophytes are predominantly coarse and asymmetrical, often extending beyond the contours of the annulus (‘non-marginal’)... Radiographic changes in the peripheral joints and spine are identical to those seen in psoriasis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: Which cytokine is specifically implicated in the pathological process of new bone formation (osteoproliferation) and syndesmophyte development in axial spondyloarthritis?
options: IL-22
IFN-α
IL-10
TGF-β
IL-1
correctOption: IL-22
optionExplanations: IL-22 is a member of the IL-10 family produced by Th17 and Th22 cells; in the context of AS, it stimulates osteoblasts and drives the formation of syndesmophytes.
IFN-α is more significant in the pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (the 'interferon signature').
IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that generally inhibits the inflammatory cascades seen in SpA.
While TGF-β is involved in fibrosis, the specific mediator highlighted for new bone formation in the SpA context is IL-22.
IL-1 is primarily a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in joint destruction and systemic symptoms, not specifically osteoproliferation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1035 (Book Page): Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in of axial spondyloarthritis.

category: Identify the cardinal clinical features of ankylosing spondylitis
statement: What is the pathological hallmark of advanced ankylosing spondylitis on a plain radiograph of the spine?
options: Bamboo spine
Gull-wing appearance
Punched-out erosions
