FGFR3 mutations are responsible for achondroplasia and are unrelated to autoimmune connective tissue diseases.
Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II alleles, specifically in the DR and DQ regions, are the most potent genetic risk factors for SLE across populations.
HLA-C variants are more specifically linked to psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis rather than SLE.
HLA-B27 is strongly associated with spondyloarthritides like ankylosing spondylitis, not Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Genetic factors play a role and the strongest region of association lies with alleles in the HLA-DR and DQ regions.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Environmental triggers like ultraviolet (UV) light are known to exacerbate Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. What is the specific cellular consequence of UV exposure that initiates the disease flare?
options: Increase in oxidative stress and cell damage
Stabilization of the internal elastic lamina
Downregulation of polyclonal T-cell activation
Induction of hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging
Activation of the RANKL pathway in osteoclasts
correctOption: Increase in oxidative stress and cell damage
optionExplanations: UV light causes direct DNA damage and oxidative stress, leading to increased apoptosis and providing a fresh supply of nuclear antigens for immune complexes.
Stabilization of the elastic lamina is irrelevant to SLE; in fact, fragmentation of the elastic lamina occurs in giant cell arteritis.
SLE flares are characterized by the upregulation, not downregulation, of polyclonal T-cell and B-cell responses.
Hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging are clinical features of a discoid rash but not the inciting mechanism of the flare itself.
The RANKL pathway is involved in bone erosions (seen in RA) but is not the primary mechanism by which UV light triggers SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In support of this, environmental factors that cause flares of SLE, such as ultraviolet light and infections, increase oxidative stress and cause cell damage.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: In the assessment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, how many criteria must be met to satisfy the standard classification requirements?
options: At least 4 of 11
At least 11 of 11
At least 3 of 11
At least 2 of 11
At least 6 of 11
correctOption: At least 4 of 11
optionExplanations: Standard classification requires 4 out of 11 clinical and immunological criteria to be met, either currently or in the past.
It is extremely rare for a patient to manifest all 11 criteria simultaneously; the criteria are designed to capture the disease's heterogeneity.
Three criteria are often found in undifferentiated connective tissue disease but do not reach the threshold for SLE diagnosis.
Meeting only 2 criteria is insufficient for a formal classification of SLE as many features overlap with other conditions.
Requiring 6 criteria would be too restrictive and would delay the diagnosis for many patients with significant multisystem disease.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): To fulfil the classification criteria for SLE, at least 4 of the 11 factors shown in Box 26.63 must be present or have occurred in the past.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Which specific ethnic population exhibits the highest estimated prevalence of SLE, reaching approximately 0.2%?
options: People of European descent
Pima Indians
People of African Caribbean origin
South Asian populations
Maori populations
correctOption: People of African Caribbean origin
optionExplanations: People of European descent have a much lower prevalence of approximately 0.03%.
Pima Indians are mentioned as having the highest prevalence of Rheumatoid Arthritis (5%), not SLE.
African Caribbean individuals have a significantly higher prevalence (0.2%) compared to Europeans, often presenting with more severe disease.
While SLE exists in South Asia, the reference text identifies the African Caribbean population as the high-prevalence group (0.2%).
Maoris are noted for higher levels of serum uric acid and gout risk, rather than a specific high prevalence of SLE in this text.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a rare disease with a prevalence that ranges from about 0.03% in people of European descent to 0.2% in people of African Caribbean origin.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A 29-year-old female presents with recurrent pleuritic chest pain and a new-onset erythematous rash on her cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. She has a known history of early-onset SLE. Genetic testing reveals a rare homozygous inherited mutation. Which protein deficiency is most likely responsible for her severe early-onset phenotype?
options: Janus Kinase 1 (JAK1)
Tumour Necrosis Factor alpha
C1q complement component
Aggrecan
Matrix Metalloproteinase 1 (MMP-1)
correctOption: C1q complement component
optionExplanations: JAK1 is a signaling molecule; while targeted by drugs, its inherited deficiency is not listed as a primary cause of SLE in the text.
TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that is often elevated in inflammatory states, not a protein whose inherited deficiency causes SLE.
Inherited deficiencies of early complement components (C1q, C2, C4) are strongly linked to the development of SLE, often with early and severe presentations.
Aggrecan is a structural component of cartilage matrix; its degradation is a feature of osteoarthritis, not the cause of SLE.
Matrix Metalloproteinases are enzymes involved in tissue degradation in RA and OA; they are not the primary genetic factor for SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In a few instances, SLE is associated with inherited mutations in complement components C1q, C2 and C4

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: In the pathological loop of SLE, how does the failure of apoptotic cell clearance contribute to the perpetuation of the immune response?
options: It leads to the exhaustion of synovial macrophages.
It triggers the rapid dissolution of monosodium urate crystals.
It prevents the presentation of HLA-DR molecules to T-cells.
It results in the inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface.
It causes the thickening of the outer joint capsule.
correctOption: It results in the inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface.
optionExplanations: While macrophages are involved in clearance, the primary pathogenic step is the exposure of antigens, not the mere 'exhaustion' of the cells.
Urate crystal dissolution is a process related to the resolution of gout and is unrelated to SLE apoptosis pathology.
The failure of clearance actually promotes antigen presentation via MHC (HLA) molecules rather than preventing it.
Persistent apoptotic material exposes nuclear components (DNA, histones) that are normally hidden, initiating an autoimmune cycle.
Capsular thickening is a feature of joint remodeling in osteoarthritis, not a component of the immune loop in SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): ...defects in apoptosis or in the clearance of apoptotic cells, which causes inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface, leading to polyclonal B- and T-cell activation, and autoantibody production.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Which DNA exonuclease has been identified as a site of inherited mutations predisposing individuals to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
options: STAT3
Jo-1
Scl70
TREX
ADAMTS-5
correctOption: TREX
optionExplanations: STAT3 is a signaling molecule associated with the risk of ankylosing spondylitis, not the primary DNA exonuclease mutation in SLE.
Jo-1 is an antibody (antisynthetase) associated with polymyositis and interstitial lung disease.
Scl70 is an antibody (anti-topoisomerase 1) used as a biomarker for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
TREX is a DNA exonuclease; mutations in its gene lead to the accumulation of endogenous DNA, triggering an interferon response and SLE.
ADAMTS-5 is a proteinase involved in cartilage degradation in osteoarthritis, not a DNA exonuclease linked to SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In a few instances, SLE is associated with inherited mutations in... the DNA exonuclease TREX.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
coreConcept: Prevalence of musculoskeletal symptoms in SLE
statement: Which of the following musculoskeletal manifestations is reported to occur in approximately 90% of patients diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
options: Marginal joint erosions
Jaccoud’s arthropathy
Chronic synovitis with joint swelling
Atlanto-axial subluxation
Arthralgia
correctOption: Arthralgia
optionExplanations: Marginal joint erosions are a hallmark of Rheumatoid Arthritis, but the text explicitly states that in SLE, 'joint erosions are not a feature.'
Jaccoud’s arthropathy refers to joint deformities resulting from tendon damage in SLE, but it is less common than simple arthralgia.
While tenosynovitis may occur, the text notes that 'clinically apparent synovitis with joint swelling is unusual' in SLE compared to other inflammatory arthritides.
Atlanto-axial subluxation is a serious complication associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis and Axial Spondyloarthritis, not typically SLE.
Arthralgia is the most prevalent musculoskeletal symptom in SLE, affecting 90% of patients, typically presenting with early morning stiffness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Arthralgia is a common symptom, occurring in 90% of patients, and is often associated with early morning stiffness.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: What is the primary underlying pathological mechanism responsible for the development of Jaccoud’s arthropathy in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Focal loss of articular cartilage and subchondral cyst development
Proteolytic degradation of the hyaline cartilage matrix
Tendon damage leading to joint deformity
Subchondral bone sclerosis and osteophyte formation
Invasion of bone by an inflamed synovial pannus
correctOption: Tendon damage leading to joint deformity
optionExplanations: Focal loss of cartilage and cysts are the defining pathological features of Osteoarthritis, whereas SLE joint involvement is primarily soft-tissue driven.
Proteolytic degradation of cartilage is a central feature of Osteoarthritis and RA, but Jaccoud’s is defined by mechanical tendon instability.
Jaccoud’s arthropathy is unique because the deformities are 'reducible' and stem from tendon laxity or damage rather than bone destruction.
Sclerosis and osteophytes are characteristic of Osteoarthritis, representing a degenerative rather than an autoimmune inflammatory process.
Synovial pannus invasion is the mechanism for erosive damage in Rheumatoid Arthritis; SLE is specifically noted to be non-erosive.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Joint deformities may arise (Jaccoud’s arthropathy) as the result of tendon damage, but joint erosions are not a feature.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: In the context of systemic lupus erythematosus, which clinical feature best differentiates secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon from the primary form found in the general population?
options: Age of onset typically occurring before 20 years
Presence of a positive family history of Raynaud’s
Bilateral symmetry of the vasospastic attacks
Presence of digital ulceration
Absence of capillary nail-fold loop changes
correctOption: Presence of digital ulceration
optionExplanations: Primary Raynaud's often begins in adolescence (under 20), whereas secondary Raynaud's in SLE typically presents after age 25.
A positive family history is more characteristic of primary Raynaud's; its absence is actually a feature suggesting a secondary cause like SLE.
While symmetry can occur in both, it does not serve as a reliable differentiator between primary and secondary pathological processes.
Digital ulceration indicates tissue ischemia and is a hallmark of secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon in autoimmune connective tissue diseases like SLE.
Secondary Raynaud's is associated with 'loss of the normal loop pattern' and 'capillary fallout,' so the absence of these would suggest the primary form.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): Features of secondary RP include age at onset of over 25 years, other features of AICTD, absence of a family history of RP, severity of symptoms, presence of digital ulceration (Fig. 26.45) and male gender.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A 24-year-old female presents with a raised erythematous rash on her cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds, accompanied by generalized fatigue. Laboratory findings reveal a low absolute lymphocyte count and significant proteinuria. Which of the following nervous system manifestations is most likely to be associated with her suspected underlying condition?
options: Visual hallucinations and organic psychosis
Symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Resting tremor and bradykinesia
Ascending paralysis and loss of deep tendon reflexes
Lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy
correctOption: Visual hallucinations and organic psychosis
optionExplanations: SLE can involve the CNS (Cerebral Lupus), presenting with psychiatric symptoms like hallucinations and organic psychosis, as well as chorea.
Proximal muscle weakness is characteristic of Polymyositis or Dermatomyositis, though SLE can cause myalgia, it is not a primary CNS feature.
Resting tremor and bradykinesia are signs of Parkinsonism, which is not a standard neurological manifestation of SLE.
Ascending paralysis is typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome, which is not a primary manifestation of central nervous system SLE.
Facial nerve palsy is a peripheral nerve issue; SLE CNS involvement focuses on central manifestations like transverse myelitis and meningitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): More specific features of cerebral SLE include visual hallucinations, chorea, organic psychosis, transverse myelitis and lymphocytic meningitis.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: Which specific mechanism is responsible for the neutropenia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia commonly observed in patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Antibody-mediated destruction of peripheral blood cells
Bone marrow suppression by chronic interleukin-6 release
Myelofibrosis caused by deposition of immune complexes in the marrow
Nutritional deficiencies secondary to mesenteric vasculitis
Sequestration of cells within an enlarged spleen (Felty Syndrome)
correctOption: Antibody-mediated destruction of peripheral blood cells
optionExplanations: The core hematological pathology in SLE is the production of autoantibodies that target and destroy circulating white cells, red cells, and platelets.
IL-6 triggers acute phase proteins in the liver in diseases like RA, but the cytopenias in SLE are specifically antibody-mediated.
Myelofibrosis is a primary bone marrow disorder; SLE hematological manifestations occur primarily in the peripheral circulation via antibodies.
While mesenteric vasculitis can occur in SLE, it leads to bowel infarction or pain, not the primary destruction of hematological lineages.
Felty Syndrome is a complication of Rheumatoid Arthritis involving splenomegaly, not the primary mechanism of cytopenias in SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): Neutropenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia may occur, due to antibody-mediated destruction of peripheral blood cells.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: Which of the following laboratory markers serves as a reliable clinical guide for assessing the current level of disease activity in systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Serum level of C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
Presence of Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies
Degree of lymphopenia
Presence of anti-centromere antibodies
Titre of Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)
correctOption: Degree of lymphopenia
optionExplanations: CRP is 'often normal in active SLE'; an elevated CRP actually suggests serositis or co-existing infection rather than purely lupus activity.
Anti-Ro antibodies are markers for certain subsets of SLE (like ANA-negative) or Sjögren's, but they do not fluctuate with disease activity.
In SLE, the absolute lymphocyte count drops as the disease becomes more active, making lymphopenia a useful marker for clinical monitoring.
Anti-centromere antibodies are characteristic biomarkers for localized cutaneous systemic sclerosis, not systemic lupus erythematosus.
ANA is a screening tool with high sensitivity but low specificity for activity; titres do not reliably track with day-to-day disease flare.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): The degree of lymphopenia can be a guide to disease activity.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: What are the characteristic findings on urine microscopy that indicate a typical renal lesion associated with systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Bence-Jones proteins and calcium oxalate crystals
Eosinophiluria and white cell casts
Sterile pyuria and glucose-6-phosphate casts
Heavy haematuria, proteinuria, and casts
Uric acid crystals and high pH
correctOption: Heavy haematuria, proteinuria, and casts
optionExplanations: Bence-Jones proteins are light chains seen in Multiple Myeloma, which can cause renal failure but via a different mechanism than SLE.
Eosinophiluria is associated with acute interstitial nephritis, often drug-induced, rather than the proliferative GN typical of SLE.
Sterile pyuria can be seen in various conditions (like TB or stones), but it is not the defining microscopic feature of lupus nephritis.
Proliferative glomerulonephritis in SLE presents with a 'nephritic' sediment including hematuria (blood), proteinuria (protein), and cellular casts.
Uric acid crystals and high pH are relevant to gout and stone formation, not the autoimmune glomerular damage seen in SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): The typical renal lesion is a proliferative glomerulonephritis, characterised by heavy haematuria, proteinuria and casts on urine microscopy.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
coreConcept: Central Nervous System Manifestations of SLE
statement: A 30-year-old patient with long-standing systemic lupus erythematosus presents with new-onset involuntary jerky movements of the limbs and visual hallucinations. Based on the known clinical manifestations of the nervous system in SLE, which pathological process is most likely occurring?
options: Cerebral involvement presenting as chorea and psychosis
Demyelination of peripheral nerves in a glove-and-stocking distribution
Compression of the spinal cord by atlanto-axial subluxation
Formation of amyloid plaques in the cerebral cortex
Infiltration of the basal ganglia by IgG4-secreting plasma cells
correctOption: Cerebral involvement presenting as chorea and psychosis
optionExplanations: Chorea (involuntary movements) and visual hallucinations (psychosis) are recognized specific central nervous system manifestations of SLE.
Peripheral neuropathy can occur, but the combination of hallucinations and chorea points to central (cerebral) rather than peripheral involvement.
Atlanto-axial subluxation is associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis; in SLE, neurological issues are usually parenchymal or meningeal, not mechanical.
Amyloidosis in rheumatology is a complication of chronic inflammation (like RA) usually affecting kidneys; amyloid plaques in the brain refer to Alzheimer's.
IgG4-secreting plasma cells are the hallmark of IgG4-related disease, which can mimic many AICTDs but is a distinct clinical entity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): More specific features of cerebral SLE include visual hallucinations, chorea, organic psychosis, transverse myelitis and lymphocytic meningitis.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging on the scalp, resulting in areas of scarring alopecia. This clinical manifestation is best described as:
options: Discoid rash
Malar rash
Urticarial eruption
Diffuse non-scarring alopecia
Livedo reticularis
correctOption: Discoid rash
optionExplanations: Discoid lesions are distinct in SLE for causing permanent damage (scarring) and specific histological features like follicular plugging.
Malar rash is an erythematous, raised facial rash that spares the nasolabial folds and does not typically cause scarring or follicular plugging.
Urticarial eruptions are wheal-like hives; they do not cause hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, or permanent scarring alopecia.
Diffuse non-scarring alopecia can occur in active SLE, but it lacks the follicular plugging and hyperkeratosis characteristic of the discoid type.
Livedo reticularis is a mottled, lace-like purplish discoloration of the skin associated with vasculitis or antiphospholipid syndrome.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): A discoid rash characterised by hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging, with scarring alopecia if it occurs on the scalp.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: Which characteristic feature of the malar facial rash in SLE helps clinically distinguish it from other conditions like rosacea?
options: Resolution only with oral antibiotics
Sparing of the nasolabial folds
Presence of comedones and pustules
Permanent scarring and skin atrophy
Involvement of the extensor surfaces of the fingers
correctOption: Sparing of the nasolabial folds
optionExplanations: Malar rashes in SLE respond to sun protection and steroids/HCQ; rosacea might respond to antibiotics, but the sparing of folds is the clinical key.
Sparing of the nasolabial folds (the creases running from the nose to the mouth) is a classic anatomical landmark for the SLE malar rash.
Comedones and pustules are features of acne or rosacea; the SLE malar rash is typically a flat or raised erythematous patch.
The malar rash in SLE typically does not cause scarring; discoid rashes cause scarring, but the malar rash usually resolves without permanent change.
Involvement of extensor surfaces of fingers (Gottron's papules) is characteristic of Dermatomyositis, not the malar rash of SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): The classic malar facial rash (up to 20% of patients). This is erythematous, raised and painful or itchy, and occurs over the cheeks with sparing of the nasolabial folds.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A comparison of epidemiological data reveals significant ethnic variations in the susceptibility to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). What is the estimated prevalence of SLE specifically among individuals of African Caribbean origin?
optionExplanations: As per the reference text, individuals of African Caribbean origin have a prevalence of 0.2%, which is more than six times higher than that of European populations.
0.03% represents the prevalence of SLE in people of European descent, which is significantly lower than the rate seen in the African Caribbean population.
0.50% is an overestimation and exceeds the documented prevalence of 0.2% for the African Caribbean population mentioned in the text.
0.10% is an incorrect figure; while higher than the European rate, it does not reach the 0.2% specified for the targeted ethnic group.
0.01% is lower than any reported prevalence in the reference text for SLE in major ethnic groups; the minimum cited is 0.03% for Europeans.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a rare disease with a prevalence that ranges from about 0.03% in people of European descent to 0.2% in people of African Caribbean origin.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Environmental triggers such as ultraviolet (UV) light and infections are known to exacerbate Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). Through which pathophysiological mechanism do these factors primarily induce autoimmune flares?
options: Reduction of the total number of circulating dendritic cells
Stabilizing apoptotic membranes to prevent antigen leak
Increasing oxidative stress leading to cellular damage
Direct inhibition of B-cell polyclonal activation
Decreasing the expression of HLA-DQ alleles on cell surfaces
correctOption: Increasing oxidative stress leading to cellular damage
optionExplanations: The text suggests these triggers activate immune pathways rather than reducing the population of essential antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells.
Environmental triggers destabilize rather than stabilize cells, promoting inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens through damaged or poorly cleared apoptotic debris.
UV light and infections increase oxidative stress, which causes cell damage. This damage leads to the exposure of intracellular and nuclear antigens that are otherwise hidden from the immune system.
UV light and infections promote, rather than inhibit, polyclonal B-cell activation by increasing the availability of self-antigens.
The expression of HLA alleles is genetically determined and potentially upregulated during inflammation, not decreased by environmental triggers.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): environmental factors that cause flares of SLE, such as ultraviolet light and infections, increase oxidative stress and cause cell damage.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: While over 100 susceptibility loci have been identified in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), the strongest genetic association is consistently observed in which of the following regions?
options: The immunoglobulin receptor FcγRIIIb tail sequence
Complement component C3 coding sequences
Alleles in the HLA-DR and DQ regions
The DNA exonuclease TREX promoter region only
Mutations in the IL-17 receptor gene
correctOption: Alleles in the HLA-DR and DQ regions
optionExplanations: FcγRIIIb is mentioned as a susceptibility locus, but the text explicitly prioritizes HLA-DR and DQ as the regions of strongest association.
Mutations in C1q, C2, and C4 are associated with SLE, but C3 is not specifically listed as an inherited complement mutation predisposing to the disease in this text.
The HLA-DR and DQ regions within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) represent the most significant genetic risk factors for SLE development.
While TREX mutations are mentioned, they are rare single-gene associations and do not constitute the 'strongest region' of general association compared to HLA.
IL-17 is more traditionally associated with spondyloarthritides and psoriasis; the text does not cite IL-17 receptors as the primary genetic locus for SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Genetic factors play a role and the strongest region of association lies with alleles in the HLA-DR and DQ regions.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A 24-year-old female presents with persistent fatigue, a butterfly-shaped facial rash that appeared after a weekend in the sun, and symmetrical joint pain in her hands. Given that the peak age of onset and female-to-male ratio align with her presentation, what is the most likely underlying immunological failure leading to her symptoms?
options: Over-clearance of apoptotic fragments by macrophages
Polyclonal T-cell suppression by ultraviolet radiation
Failure of the nasolabial folds to express MHC class II
Mutation-driven exhaustion of the DNA exonuclease TREX
Inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface
correctOption: Inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface
optionExplanations: The pathogenesis involves the *failure* or defect in clearance, not over-clearance, leading to the persistence of antigenic material.
Ultraviolet radiation leads to cell damage and immune *activation*, not suppression of the T-cell response in the context of SLE flares.
Malar rash typically *spares* the nasolabial folds, but this is a clinical observation of the rash pattern, not the underlying immunological failure of the disease.
While TREX is involved in some cases, the generalized mechanism of SLE flares and antigen exposure described is broader than just TREX exhaustion.
Defects in clearing apoptotic cells lead to the exposure of nuclear and intracellular components. These act as autoantigens, triggering the polyclonal immune response characteristic of SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): SLE may occur because of defects in apoptosis or in the clearance of apoptotic cells, which causes inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface, leading to polyclonal B- and T-cell activation

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: The pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) involves a complex interplay between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors. Which rare inherited complement deficiency is specifically identified as a genetic risk factor for the disease?
options: Complement components C1q, C2, and C4
C5-C9 deficiency leading to neisserial infections
Complement C3 and C5 deficiency
Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) assembly defects
Factor H and Factor I mutations
correctOption: Complement components C1q, C2, and C4
optionExplanations: Inherited deficiencies in C1q, C2, and C4 are linked to SLE, likely due to their roles in the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells.
Late complement component deficiencies (C5-C9) primarily increase susceptibility to Neisseria, not SLE, as per the focused etiology in the text.
C3 and C5 are central to the complement cascade, but the text specifically identifies the early classic pathway components as SLE risk factors.
MAC assembly (C5b-9) is involved in cell lysis; its deficiency is not the stated genetic risk for SLE according to the reference material.
Factor H and I are regulatory proteins of the alternative pathway, not the specific complement components listed as inherited SLE risks in the text.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In a few instances, SLE is associated with inherited mutations in complement components C1q, C2 and C4

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Regarding the demographic distribution of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), which of the following statistics accurately reflects the gender predominance of the disease?
options: 90% of affected patients are female
50% of affected patients are female
60% of affected patients are female
80% of affected patients are female
75% of affected patients are female
correctOption: 90% of affected patients are female
optionExplanations: SLE is overwhelmingly common in females, with 90% of cases occurring in women, particularly during their reproductive years.
A 50% distribution would imply no gender bias, which is incorrect given the strong female predominance in SLE.
60% is far lower than the actual clinical and textbook incidence of the disease in females.
80% is incorrect; the specific figure provided in the authoritative text is 90%.
75% is an underestimate; while many autoimmune diseases show female bias, SLE is particularly extreme at 9:1.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Some 90% of affected patients are female and the peak age at onset is between 20 and 30 years.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: An elite researcher is studying the heritability of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). Based on established genetic studies, what is the estimated contribution of genetic factors to the total susceptibility (heritability) of the disease?
optionExplanations: 10%–20% would suggest that environmental factors are almost entirely responsible, which underestimates the significant genetic component found in HLA studies.
20%–40% is lower than the estimate provided in the reference text.
90%–100% would suggest a purely Mendelian disorder, whereas SLE is a complex polygenic disease with strong environmental triggers.
The text states heritability is 40%–60%, indicating that genes and environment contribute roughly equally to the risk profile.
70%–80% would imply a much higher genetic control, similar to Psoriatic Arthritis, but SLE has a larger environmental influence.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): The overall heritability of SLE has been estimated to be about 40%–60%, illustrating the importance of environmental influences

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A 19-year-old female presents with a new onset of malar rash, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. Family history is significant for a brother with an unspecified autoimmune disorder. Given the early age of onset and severity, the clinician suspects a rare single-gene mutation. Which enzyme deficiency is mentioned as a rare genetic cause of SLE?
options: Peptidylarginine deiminase 4
Matrix metalloproteinase-9
DNA exonuclease TREX
Superoxide dismutase
Xanthine oxidase
correctOption: DNA exonuclease TREX
optionExplanations: PAD4 is involved in citrullination (relevant to Rheumatoid Arthritis) but is not the enzyme linked to rare monogenic SLE in this text.
Matrix metalloproteinases are involved in tissue remodeling (e.g., in RA or OA) but are not cited as a monogenic cause of SLE.
Mutations in the TREX gene (DNA exonuclease) lead to an accumulation of nucleic acids, which can trigger interferon pathways and lead to SLE.
Superoxide dismutase deals with oxidative stress, but its inherited mutation is not listed in the text as a primary genetic risk for SLE.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in uric acid metabolism and gout, not the genetic susceptibility to SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In a few instances, SLE is associated with inherited mutations... in the DNA exonuclease TREX.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Oxidative stress is a critical component in the environmental triggering of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. According to the pathophysiological model, how does increased oxidative stress from UV light or infection specifically lead to B-cell activation?
options: By depleting serum complement C1q levels directly
By causing a shift from IgG to IgM production
By inhibiting T-cell receptors through nitric oxide release
By damaging cells and exposing intracellular antigens
By preventing the formation of immune complexes
correctOption: By damaging cells and exposing intracellular antigens
optionExplanations: While C1q deficiency is a risk factor, oxidative stress doesn't directly 'deplete' it as its primary pathogenic route mentioned in the text.
The text does not mention an 'IgG to IgM shift' as a mechanism for flare induction following oxidative stress damage.
The text focuses on activation of the immune system (polyclonal B and T-cell activation) rather than inhibition of T-cell receptors.
Oxidative stress causes cell damage, which results in the presentation of intracellular antigens to the immune system, fueling autoantibody production.
Increased oxidative stress and antigen exposure *promote* the formation of immune complexes, which then cause tissue damage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): UV light and infections, increase oxidative stress and cause cell damage. Whatever the underlying cause, autoantibody production and immune complex formation are thought to be important mechanisms of tissue damage

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Genetic variants in the regulation of the immune response are central to SLE susceptibility. Besides the HLA region, which specific receptor variant is highlighted as a susceptibility locus for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
options: Interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R)
T-cell receptor alpha chain variable region
Tumour Necrosis Factor receptor 1 (TNFR1)
IgA Fc receptor (FcαRI)
Immunoglobulin receptor FcγRIIIb
correctOption: Immunoglobulin receptor FcγRIIIb
optionExplanations: While IL-6 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in many arthritic diseases, its receptor is not the specific locus mentioned for SLE risk here.
T-cell receptor polymorphisms are not the primary non-HLA loci emphasized in this section of the text for SLE risk.
TNFR1 mutations are associated with other periodic fever syndromes, but the text specifically names FcγRIIIb for SLE.
FcαRI (IgA receptor) is not identified in the provided text as a specific genetic susceptibility locus for SLE.
The FcγRIIIb receptor variant is specifically listed in the text as one of the key non-HLA genetic factors predisposing individuals to SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): SLE is associated with inherited mutations... in the immunoglobulin receptor FcγRIIIb

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Which of the following demographic profiles represents the peak incidence and highest prevalence group for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)?
options: Post-menopausal women of European descent
Males with a history of occupational silica exposure
Females between the ages of 20 and 30 years
Children under the age of 16 years
Males in their fourth and fifth decades
correctOption: Females between the ages of 20 and 30 years
optionExplanations: SLE prevalence is actually higher in women of African Caribbean origin (0.2%) compared to those of European descent (0.03%), and it peaks before menopause.
Silica exposure is a known trigger for systemic sclerosis-like diseases but is not the primary risk factor or demographic defining the peak incidence of SLE.
SLE is remarkably female-dominant (9:1 ratio) and typically presents during the peak of reproductive years (20-30), suggesting a significant hormonal influence on its onset.
While juvenile-onset SLE exists and often carries more severe renal involvement, it is less common than the peak adult onset in the third decade of life.
Systemic sclerosis typically peaks in the fourth and fifth decades, but SLE peaks much earlier, primarily in younger women during their childbearing years.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a rare disease with a prevalence that ranges from about 0.03% in people of European descent to 0.2% in people of African Caribbean origin. Some 90% of affected patients are female and the peak age at onset is between 20 and 30 years.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: According to current pathophysiological theories, which cellular mechanism is primarily compromised in SLE, leading to the inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens?
options: Defects in apoptosis or the clearance of apoptotic cells
Increased production of Interleukin-17 by Th17 cells
Accelerated fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition
Impaired intestinal mucosal barrier integrity
Over-activation of the RANKL pathway in osteoclasts
correctOption: Defects in apoptosis or the clearance of apoptotic cells
optionExplanations: The failure to efficiently clear apoptotic debris allows intracellular contents (like nuclear DNA/proteins) to persist and be presented to the immune system, breaking self-tolerance.
While IL-17 and Th17 cells play roles in many inflammatory conditions like psoriasis and AxSpA, the foundational deficit in SLE is the handling of apoptotic cells.
Accelerated fibroblast activity is the hallmark of systemic sclerosis, causing tissue induration and fibrosis, rather than the primary immune deficit in SLE.
Impaired mucosal integrity and interaction with gut microbiota are strongly linked to the spondyloarthritides (axSpA) rather than the central mechanism of SLE.
RANKL pathway activation is a feature of bone erosion in rheumatoid arthritis and some spondyloarthropathies, but it does not drive the initial antigen exposure in SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): This has led to the hypothesis that SLE may occur because of defects in apoptosis or in the clearance of apoptotic cells, which causes inappropriate exposure of intracellular antigens on the cell surface, leading to polyclonal B- and T-cell activation.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A 22-year-old female patient presents with cold-induced digital color changes. Which clinical finding would most strongly suggest that this is a secondary phenomenon related to an autoimmune connective tissue disease like SLE rather than primary Raynaud’s phenomenon?
options: Symmetric involvement of the digits without ulceration
Age of onset under 20 years
Resolution of symptoms upon warming the hands
The presence of digital ulceration
Presence of a positive family history of Raynaud's
correctOption: The presence of digital ulceration
optionExplanations: Primary Raynaud's is typically symmetric and benign; secondary Raynaud's associated with SLE often shows signs of actual tissue ischemia and damage.
Primary Raynaud's often begins in teenage years or early adulthood (under 20). Onset after age 25 is a red flag for a secondary underlying autoimmune disease.
Both primary and secondary Raynaud's typically resolve or improve with rewarming; this does not distinguish between the two etiologies.
Digital ulceration indicates significant vasculopathy and tissue ischemia, which are characteristic of secondary Raynaud's in diseases like SLE or systemic sclerosis.
A positive family history is more characteristic of primary Raynaud's, which is a benign, often inherited disorder in the general population.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): Features of secondary RP include age at onset of over 25 years, other features of AICTD, absence of a family history of RP, severity of symptoms, presence of digital ulceration and male gender.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: A 26-year-old woman of African Caribbean origin is diagnosed with SLE. Based on population-based genome studies, what is the estimated heritability of this condition, reflecting the genetic component of her risk?
options: Exactly 100% in monozygotic twins
Less than 5%
optionExplanations: Even in monozygotic twins, concordance is not 100%, as environmental influences and epigenetic changes are required to trigger the disease phenotype.
Heritability exceeding 80% is associated with psoriatic arthritis rather than SLE, which has a more significant environmental interplay.
SLE is a complex polygenic disease where genetic factors account for roughly half the risk (40-60%), while environmental triggers account for the remainder.
The value of 12-15% refers to the concordance rate of rheumatoid arthritis in monozygotic twins, not the overall heritability estimate for SLE.
A heritability of less than 5% would imply the disease is almost entirely environmental, which contradicts the known association with HLA-DR and DQ alleles.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): The overall heritability of SLE has been estimated to be about 40%–60%, illustrating the importance of environmental influences, although the nature of these are unclear.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Environmental triggers like ultraviolet (UV) light are known to cause exacerbations in SLE patients. What is the specific mechanism by which these factors contribute to tissue damage and flares?
options: Reduction in the concentration of complement components C3 and C4
Suppression of anti-dsDNA antibody production
Stabilization of apoptotic cell clearance mechanisms
Direct inhibition of B-cell and T-cell polyclonal activation
Increased oxidative stress and induction of cell damage
correctOption: Increased oxidative stress and induction of cell damage
optionExplanations: While complement may be consumed during a flare, the immediate mechanism of the UV trigger is the induction of oxidative stress and cell death.
Environmental triggers like UV light generally lead to an increase in autoantibody production, not a suppression.
UV light destabilizes cellular processes and increases the load of apoptotic cells, overwhelming already defective clearance mechanisms in SLE patients.
UV light actually promotes the activation of B and T cells by increasing the availability of self-antigens through cell damage.
UV radiation causes DNA damage and oxidative stress in keratinocytes, leading to apoptosis and the release of intracellular antigens that trigger immune responses.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In support of this, environmental factors that cause flares of SLE, such as ultraviolet light and infections, increase oxidative stress and cause cell damage.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: In the classification of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, how many of the eleven standard criteria must be present, either simultaneously or sequentially, to satisfy the diagnosis?
options: At least 2
At least 6
All 11
Exactly 7
At least 4
correctOption: At least 4
optionExplanations: Two criteria are insufficient for the classification of SLE, as many individual features (like arthralgia or ANA) can occur in other diseases.
A score of 6 or more is the threshold for the diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis according to EULAR/ACR 2010 criteria, not SLE.
Requiring all 11 criteria is impossible, as many patients have predominantly skin-joint disease or predominantly renal-CNS disease, rarely all simultaneously.
A requirement of 7 criteria would be far too stringent, potentially missing many patients with significant, life-threatening organ involvement.
The 11 criteria (Box 26.63) cover various systems; meeting at least 4 provides high specificity for the classification of SLE in clinical research and diagnosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): To fulfil the classification criteria for SLE, at least 4 of the 11 factors shown in Box 26.63 must be present or have occurred in the past.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Specific inherited mutations in the classical complement pathway can predispose an individual to developing SLE. Which group of complement components is specifically associated with these inherited mutations in SLE pathogenesis?
options: Properdin and Factor B
C1q, C2, and C4
C5, C6, and C7
C8 and C9
C3 and Factor D
correctOption: C1q, C2, and C4
optionExplanations: Properdin and Factor B are part of the alternative pathway; their deficiency is not a classically recognized major genetic risk factor for SLE.
Deficiencies in early classical pathway components (C1q, C2, C4) impair the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells, directly contributing to SLE risk.
C5-C7 are part of the terminal membrane attack complex; deficiencies here primarily predispose to Neisserial infections rather than SLE.
Deficiencies in C8 and C9 impair the completion of the membrane attack complex but are not associated with the loss of self-tolerance seen in SLE.
While low C3 levels are found in active disease due to consumption, primary inherited deficiency of classical components C1q/C2/C4 is the key genetic risk mentioned.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): In a few instances, SLE is associated with inherited mutations in complement components C1q, C2 and C4...

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis: Malar Rash vs Rosacea
statement: A 28-year-old female presents with an erythematous rash over her cheeks. To distinguish the classic SLE malar rash from a mimicking condition like rosacea, which anatomical feature is most critical to evaluate?
options: The restriction of the rash to the scalp
The involvement of the ear helix
The involvement of the forehead
The sparing of the nasolabial folds
The presence of scaling and hyperkeratosis
correctOption: The sparing of the nasolabial folds
optionExplanations: Restriction to the scalp is characteristic of alopecia or discoid lupus, whereas the malar rash is centrally facial by definition.
Ear helix involvement (Chilblain lupus or tophi) is helpful for other diagnoses, but the nasolabial fold sparing is the classic differentiator for the malar rash.
Forehead involvement can occur in both, but it is not the defining spatial characteristic that separates the two conditions.
The malar rash of SLE characteristically spares the nasolabial folds, whereas rosacea typically involves these folds, providing a high-yield diagnostic contrast.
Scaling and hyperkeratosis are features of a discoid rash, another type of lupus skin involvement, but not the defining trait of the malar 'butterfly' rash.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): The classic malar facial rash (up to 20% of patients). This is erythematous, raised and painful or itchy, and occurs over the cheeks with sparing of the nasolabial folds (Fig. 26.46). Rosacea may mimic this rash.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: The development of autoantibodies in SLE, which leads to tissue damage and vasculitis, is preceded by the activation of which immune cell populations due to the exposure of intracellular antigens?
options: Monoclonal plasma cell expansion
Selective Th17 cell suppression
Eosinophil and basophil degranulation
Polyclonal B- and T-cell activation
Osteoclast and fibroblast inhibition
correctOption: Polyclonal B- and T-cell activation
optionExplanations: SLE involves polyclonal activation, meaning many different clones of cells are activated against various antigens, unlike the monoclonal expansion in multiple myeloma.
SLE involves activation of immune pathways; suppression of Th17 is not the driving mechanism of autoantibody production in this disease context.
Eosinophil activation is more characteristic of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA) rather than the primary mechanism of SLE.
The exposure of self-antigens leads to the widespread activation of both B cells (producing antibodies) and T cells (providing help and causing direct damage).
Fibroblasts are activated in systemic sclerosis, and osteoclasts in RA; SLE pathophysiology is centered on B and T cell dysregulation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1038 (Book Page): This has led to the hypothesis that SLE may occur because of defects in apoptosis... leading to polyclonal B- and T-cell activation, and autoantibody production.

category: List common risk factors and triggers (genetic, environmental, hormonal) of SLE
statement: Aside from complement pathway genes, mutations in which specific enzyme are identified as an inherited risk factor for the development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
options: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
DNA exonuclease TREX
Matrix metalloproteinase-5
Peptidyl arginine deiminase
Xanthine oxidase
correctOption: DNA exonuclease TREX
optionExplanations: ACE inhibitors are used to treat renal crises in systemic sclerosis, but the enzyme itself is not the specific genetic mutation listed for SLE risk.
TREX is a DNA exonuclease; mutations here lead to improper handling of nucleic acids, facilitating the autoimmune response against DNA found in SLE.
ADAMTS-5 and MMPs are involved in cartilage degradation in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, not the genetic susceptibility to SLE.
Citrullination enzymes (PAD) are high-yield in Rheumatoid Arthritis (ACPAs), but TREX is the enzyme specifically linked to inherited SLE in this text.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in uric acid metabolism and is the target for gout treatments like allopurinol, not a risk factor for SLE.

Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe, life-threatening, or organ-threatening disease such as lupus nephritis or CNS involvement, not mild skin/joint disease.
Pulse steroids are indicated for acute renal or neurological crises, not as baseline therapy for musculoskeletal or cutaneous SLE.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): Patients with mild disease restricted to skin and joints can sometimes be managed with analgesics, NSAIDs and HCQ. Frequently , however , glucocorticoids are also necessary...

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: According to the classification criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), how many of the 11 established factors must be present, either serially or simultaneously, to confirm a diagnosis?
options: At least 6
Exactly 7
All 11
At least 4
At least 3
correctOption: At least 4
optionExplanations: Six criteria is the threshold for Rheumatoid Arthritis (using the 2010 EULAR/ACR score), not SLE.
Exactly seven is not a standard threshold in any major rheumatological classification system mentioned in the text.
Requiring all 11 criteria would result in a massive under-diagnosis, as few patients exhibit every possible system manifestation simultaneously.
The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria require 4 out of 11 specific clinical and laboratory findings to classify a patient as having SLE.
Three criteria are insufficient; while the patient may have 'lupus-like' features, the standard classification requires more for a formal diagnosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): To fulfil the classification criteria for SLE, at least 4 of the 11 factors shown in Box 26.63 must be present or have occurred in the past.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: In a patient with active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, what is the clinical significance of a significantly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP)?
options: It confirms the presence of Anti-dsDNA antibodies
It indicates the presence of co-existing infection or serositis
It suggests the degree of lymphopenia
It reflects the consumption of C3 and C4 complements
It is a specific marker for active lupus nephritis
correctOption: It indicates the presence of co-existing infection or serositis
optionExplanations: Anti-dsDNA is a serological autoantibody test and is not correlated with CRP levels.
Because SLE is one of the few inflammatory states where CRP stays low despite high activity, a high CRP must trigger a search for infection or serositis (pleurisy/pericarditis).
Lymphopenia is monitored via Full Blood Count (FBC) and is independent of CRP levels.
Complement consumption (low C3/C4) is a hallmark of active SLE, but it is typically associated with a high ESR and low/normal CRP, not high CRP.
Lupus nephritis typically elevates the ESR and leads to urine sediment changes, but CRP remains notoriously normal or low in uncomplicated active lupus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): CRP is often normal in active SLE and presence of an elevated CRP in SLE raises the possibility of either serositis, or co-existing infection.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A 30-year-old female presents with reducible ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities of the fingers. Radiographs of the hands reveal no marginal erosions or loss of joint space. This clinical entity, commonly associated with SLE, is known as:
options: Sclerodactyly
Psoriatic arthritis mutilans
Rheumatoid-like erosive arthritis
Boutonniere deformity
Jaccoud's arthropathy
correctOption: Jaccoud's arthropathy
optionExplanations: Sclerodactyly refers to the thickening and tightening of the skin over the fingers, typically seen in Systemic Sclerosis, not the joint laxity of SLE.
Arthritis mutilans is a highly destructive, erosive form of Psoriatic Arthritis with 'telescoping' digits, the opposite of the non-erosive SLE presentation.
Erosive arthritis is the hallmark of Rheumatoid Arthritis; its absence is what defines Jaccoud's arthropathy in SLE.
Boutonniere deformity is a specific finger position that can be part of several arthropathies, but the overall syndrome described is Jaccoud's.
Jaccoud's arthropathy is characteristic of SLE; unlike Rheumatoid Arthritis, the deformities are caused by laxity and tendon damage and are notably non-erosive on X-ray.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): Joint deformities may arise (Jaccoud’s arthropathy) as the result of tendon damage, but joint erosions are not a feature.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: The development of vasculitis and multi-organ damage in active SLE is primarily driven by which physiological 'loop' involving autoantibodies?
options: Formation of immune complexes and subsequent tissue deposition
Activation of the RANKL pathway by T-cells leading to osteoclastogenesis
Inhibition of the xanthine oxidase enzyme reducing uric acid conversion
Neutralization of nerve growth factors leading to hyperalgesia
Release of Matrix Metalloproteinases from synovial fibroblasts
correctOption: Formation of immune complexes and subsequent tissue deposition
optionExplanations: SLE is the prototype of an immune-complex-mediated disease (Type III Hypersensitivity). Autoantibodies bind to antigens, and these complexes deposit in vessels and organs, triggering inflammation.
RANKL pathways are crucial in the bone erosions of Rheumatoid Arthritis, which are notably absent in typical SLE joint involvement.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition is the mechanism of Allopurinol in treating gout, unrelated to the inflammatory loop of SLE.
Nerve growth factor inhibition is a novel therapy for osteoarthritis pain, not a mechanism of SLE-related organ damage.
MMPs and ADAMTS-5 are the primary mediators of cartilage destruction in RA and Osteoarthritis; SLE damage is driven more by systemic immune complex vasculitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): Whatever the underlying cause, autoantibody production and immune complex formation are thought to be important mechanisms of tissue damage in active SLE, leading to vasculitis and organ damage.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: In the serological evaluation of SLE, which autoantibody is characterized as being highly specific for the disease and useful for monitoring disease activity?
options: Anti-dsDNA
Anti-Sm (Smith)
Anti-La (SS-B)
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)
Anti-Ro (SS-A)
correctOption: Anti-dsDNA
optionExplanations: Anti-dsDNA antibodies have high specificity for SLE and their titers often correlate with disease activity, especially in lupus nephritis.
While Anti-Sm is also very specific for SLE, it is only present in a minority of patients and does not fluctuate as reliably with disease activity as Anti-dsDNA.
Anti-La is primarily associated with Sjögren’s syndrome and is usually found in conjunction with Anti-Ro.
ANA is highly sensitive (positive in 95% of cases) but lacks specificity, as it can be positive in many other autoimmune conditions and even healthy individuals.
Anti-Ro is associated with SLE but also Sjögren’s syndrome and neonatal lupus; it is not specific for SLE alone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): Anti-dsDNA antibodies are positive in most patients and are quite specific for SLE.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A 26-year-old female presents with chronic joint pain and symmetrical deformities of the hands. Radiographic imaging reveals no marginal erosions or loss of joint space, despite significant ulnar deviation. Which of the following is the most likely clinical manifestation described?
options: Osteoarthritic nodal remodeling
Jaccoud’s arthropathy
Erosive rheumatoid-like arthritis
Septic arthritis cluster
Boutonnière deformity secondary to pannus
correctOption: Jaccoud’s arthropathy
optionExplanations: Osteoarthritic nodal remodeling involves Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes, which are distinct from the inflammatory systemic pattern of SLE.

Jaccoud’s arthropathy in SLE is caused by tendon and ligamentous laxity or damage rather than bone destruction. This leads to reducible deformities without the marginal erosions seen in other inflammatory arthritides.
Erosive arthritis is characteristic of Rheumatoid Arthritis, where pannus invades bone. In SLE, joint involvement is classically non-erosive.
Septic arthritis presents as an acute, usually monoarticular, destructive process with systemic signs of infection, unlike the chronic, non-erosive symmetrical pattern of SLE joints.
Boutonnière deformity in RA involves pannus-mediated destruction of the central slip. While SLE can show similar shapes, the underlying pathology is tendinous, not erosive.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): Arthralgia is a common symptom, occurring in 90% of patients... Joint deformities may arise (Jaccoud’s arthropathy) as the result of tendon damage, but joint erosions are not a feature.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: In patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus presenting with secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon, which pathophysiological finding during nail-fold capillaroscopy most strongly suggests an underlying autoimmune connective tissue disease over a primary idiopathic process?
options: Rapid capillary refill without structural change
Symmetrical hyperemic capillary flush
Increased density of uniform filiform capillaries
Enhanced venous return through superficial plexuses
Loss of normal loop pattern with dilatation and branching
correctOption: Loss of normal loop pattern with dilatation and branching
optionExplanations: Rapid refill is a functional hemodynamic observation; secondary Raynaud's is defined by structural microvascular remodeling and 'fallout'.
Symmetrical flushing is a physiological response to rewarming and does not indicate the microvascular architectural damage seen in SLE.
Increased density is not typical; rather, 'fallout' or areas of avascularity are expected in secondary Raynaud's phenomenon associated with connective tissue diseases.
Venous return changes are not the specific diagnostic markers for the microvascular capillary bed destruction described in autoimmune sclerotic or lupus-related vasculopathy.

In SLE and other AICTDs, the microvasculature undergoes significant structural distortion. The loss of the regular loop pattern and the presence of enlarged, branched (megacapillaries) or missing (fallout) loops are hallmark signs of secondary Raynaud's.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): Examination of capillary nail-fold loops using an ophthalmoscope... can show loss of the normal loop pattern, with capillary ‘fallout’ and dilatation and branching of loops; these features support a diagnosis of secondary RP.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient for a facial rash to differentiate Systemic Lupus Erythematosus from rosacea. Which clinical feature of the rash is most characteristic of the malar eruption seen in SLE?
options: Sparing of the nasolabial folds
Irreversible scarring and follicular plugging
Extension into the nasolabial folds
Association with thick, yellow-brown crusts
Presence of pustules and comedones
correctOption: Sparing of the nasolabial folds
optionExplanations: The malar 'butterfly' rash of SLE typically involves the bridge of the nose and the malar eminences but distinctly spares the nasolabial folds, a key diagnostic differentiator from other facial dermatoses.
Scarring and follicular plugging are hallmarks of discoid lupus (chronic cutaneous lupus), not the acute malar rash, which typically resolves without scarring.
Rashes that involve the nasolabial folds are more common in seborrheic dermatitis or rosacea; SLE classically spares these areas.
Thick crusts are characteristic of discoid lupus hyperkeratosis or impetigo, whereas the malar rash is a flatter, more acute inflammatory lesion.
Pustules are more indicative of acne or rosacea. The malar rash in SLE is typically an erythematous, raised patch without primary pustulation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): The classic malar facial rash (up to 20% of patients). This is erythematous, raised and painful or itchy, and occurs over the cheeks with sparing of the nasolabial folds.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A 25-year-old female of African Caribbean origin presents with fatigue, weight loss, and painful swelling of the wrists and knees. Examination reveals a raised erythematous rash on the cheeks and lower limb edema. Laboratory tests show proteinuria, hematuria, and a total lymphocyte count of 0.8 x 10^9/L. Which complication is the most critical determinant of her prognosis?
options: Malar dermal hypersensitivity
Secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon
Jaccoud’s arthropathy of the knees
Non-scarring diffuse alopecia
Proliferative glomerulonephritis
correctOption: Proliferative glomerulonephritis
optionExplanations: Malar rash is a diagnostic criterion but, unlike kidney disease, it does not lead to organ failure or significant mortality risks.
Raynaud’s phenomenon is common and can lead to digital ulcers, but it is rarely the primary determinant of overall life expectancy compared to internal organ damage.
While Jaccoud's arthropathy causes functional morbidity, it does not typically affect survival or long-term systemic prognosis.
Alopecia is a common dermatological feature of SLE flares but is considered a cosmetic or minor clinical manifestation in the context of systemic disease.

Renal involvement, specifically proliferative glomerulonephritis, is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in SLE. The presence of lower limb edema, proteinuria, and hematuria strongly suggests lupus nephritis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): Renal involvement is one of the main determinants of prognosis... The typical renal lesion is a proliferative glomerulonephritis, characterised by heavy haematuria, proteinuria and casts.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A patient with severe Lupus Nephritis is prescribed a regimen of pulsed intravenous cyclophosphamide. To mitigate the risk of a specific urological toxicity associated with this drug's metabolites, which agent must be co-prescribed?
options: Mesna
Belimumab
Hydroxychloroquine
Mycophenolate mofetil
Azathioprine
correctOption: Mesna
optionExplanations: Mesna binds to acrolein, the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide, preventing it from causing hemorrhagic cystitis in the bladder lining.
Belimumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting B-lymphocyte stimulator and is not a protective agent against chemical drug toxicities.
Hydroxychloroquine is used for mild to moderate skin and joint disease but does not protect the bladder from cyclophosphamide metabolites.
Mycophenolate mofetil is an alternative to cyclophosphamide for inducing remission but is not used specifically to mitigate cyclophosphamide's side effects.
Azathioprine is primarily used for maintenance therapy; it does not have a role in preventing the acute urological complications of cyclophosphamide therapy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis, but the risk can be minimised by good hydration and co-prescription of mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate), which binds its urotoxic metabolites.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: Which of the following skin manifestations of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus is uniquely characterized by hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, and the potential for scarring alopecia?
options: Photosensitive erythematous patches
Urticarial eruptions
Malar facial rash
Livedo reticularis
Discoid rash
correctOption: Discoid rash
optionExplanations: Photosensitive patches are acute reactions to UV light; while they occur in SLE, they lack the specific chronic morphology of discoid lupus like follicular plugging.
Urticarial eruptions in SLE are transient wheals related to inflammation or vasculitis and do not lead to scarring or hyperkeratotic changes.
The malar rash is typically an acute inflammatory eruption that resolves without the permanent scarring or hyperkeratosis seen in discoid lesions.
Livedo reticularis is a mottled vascular pattern related to hypercoagulability (Antiphospholipid syndrome) or vasculitis, not a hyperkeratotic scarring process.
Discoid lupus is a chronic form of cutaneous lupus that leads to localized tissue destruction, including keratin plugs in hair follicles and irreversible scarring of the scalp dermis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): A discoid rash characterised by hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging, with scarring alopecia if it occurs on the scalp.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A patient with SLE is undergoing routine hematological monitoring. The clinician observes that the lymphocyte count has dropped significantly compared to the baseline from the previous month. How should this finding be clinically interpreted based on the disease’s hematological manifestations?
options: As evidence of secondary bacterial infection
As a sign of resolving serositis
As an expected response to antimalarial therapy
As a guide to increasing disease activity
As an indicator of drug-induced bone marrow suppression only
correctOption: As a guide to increasing disease activity
optionExplanations: Bacterial infections usually present with a neutrophil leukocytosis, whereas SLE itself is associated with leukopenia/lymphopenia during flares.
Serositis (like pleurisy) typically causes a rise in inflammatory markers (ESR) rather than a drop in lymphocytes as a sign of resolution.
Antimalarials like hydroxychloroquine are usually lymphocyte-sparing and do not typically cause significant drops in counts in routine doses.
Lymphopenia in SLE is often mediated by anti-lymphocyte antibodies and sequestering of cells; its severity often fluctuates with the overall inflammatory burden of the systemic flare.
While drugs can cause suppression, the text specifically highlights lymphopenia as a primary manifestation of the disease itself, tied to its activity levels.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): Neutropenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia may occur... The degree of lymphopenia can be a guide to disease activity.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: A 30-year-old female with a history of malar rash and arthralgia presents to the emergency department with sudden onset visual hallucinations, involuntary choreiform movements of the limbs, and severe fatigue. Laboratory tests show high-titer anti-dsDNA and low C3 levels. Which system involvement is primarily responsible for these symptoms?
options: Dermatological toxin release
Musculoskeletal metabolic imbalance
Central nervous system lupus
Secondary Sjögr en syndrome
Ocular vasculitis
correctOption: Central nervous system lupus
optionExplanations: Lupus rashes are inflammatory but do not release toxins that cause specific central neurologic movement disorders like chorea.
Metabolic imbalances in SLE (like renal failure) can cause encephalopathy, but chorea is a more specific neuro-inflammatory manifestation of the CNS itself.

Neuropsychiatric SLE (Cerebral Lupus) encompasses a range of severe manifestations including movement disorders like chorea and psychiatric symptoms like hallucinations or psychosis, often associated with active serology.
Sjögr en syndrome causes sicca symptoms (dry eyes/mouth); while it can coexist with SLE, it does not typically present with acute chorea or hallucinations.
Ocular vasculitis might cause visual loss or redness but would not explain the generalized chorea or psychiatric manifestations like hallucinations.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): More specific features of cerebral SLE include visual hallucinations, chorea, organic psychosis, transverse myelitis and lymphocytic meningitis.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
coreConcept: Acute Phase Reactant Discordance in SLE
statement: During a suspected flare of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus involving the pleura and joints, a laboratory panel shows a markedly elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) but a surprisingly normal C-reactive protein (CRP). What is the physiological significance of this discordance in SLE?
options: It suggests the flare is actually a concealed bacterial infection
It proves the patient has inherited C4 deficiency
It is typical of active SLE unless serositis or infection co-exists
It reflects the immediate clearance of immune complexes
It indicates the development of amyloidosis
correctOption: It is typical of active SLE unless serositis or infection co-exists
optionExplanations: Bacterial infections usually drive both ESR and CRP high; a normal CRP in an SLE patient often points toward the primary disease rather than infection.
Inherited C4 deficiency is a risk factor for developing SLE, but it is diagnosed via complement assays, not through the discordance between ESR and CRP.

In SLE, the CRP often stays low or normal even when the ESR is high. A rise in CRP in an SLE patient is a red flag that usually signifies either a secondary infection or specifically serositis (pleurisy/pericarditis).

While immune complex clearance is a central pathophysiological issue, the specific discordance of acute phase reactants is a clinical observation of protein production by the liver in response to specific cytokines.
Amyloidosis is a rare complication of chronic inflammation but is not the primary physiological reason for the ESR/CRP discordance observed in acute flares.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1041 (Book Page): CRP is often normal in active SLE and presence of an elevated CRP in SLE raises the possibility of either serositis, or co-existing infection.

category: Identify the clinical manifestations involving skin, joints, kidneys, hematological and nervous systems in SLE
statement: Which specific autoantibody is highly associated with SLE and can be used to monitor disease flares, particularly when renal involvement is suspected?
options: Anti-La (SS-B)
Anti-dsDNA antibody
Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-topoisomerase 1
Anti-Jo-1
correctOption: Anti-dsDNA antibody
optionExplanations: Anti-La is found in Sjögr en syndrome and SLE, but it is not as specific as anti-dsDNA and is not typically used to track renal flares.
Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and titers often fluctuate with disease activity, particularly correlating with the severity of lupus nephritis.
Anti-centromere antibodies are biomarkers for localized cutaneous systemic sclerosis and CREST syndrome, not SLE.
Anti-topoisomerase 1 (Scl70) is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and interstitial lung disease.
Anti-Jo-1 is an antisynthetase antibody associated with polymyositis and interstitial lung disease, not SLE.
