category: Outline the management strategies including symptomatic treatment and prevention of complications of systemic sclerosis
statement: Which biomarker is considered highly specific for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSScl) and the CREST variant?
options: Anticentromere antibodies
Anti-RNP antibodies
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies
Anti-dsDNA antibodies
Anti-Ro (SS-A) antibodies
correctOption: Anticentromere antibodies
optionExplanations: Anticentromere antibodies are the classic serological marker for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSScl) and are specifically associated with the CREST syndrome symptoms.
Anti-RNP antibodies are markers for Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD) and are not specific for the CREST variant of limited SSc.
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are antisynthetase antibodies specifically associated with polymyositis and interstitial lung disease in myositis.
Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and do not define subsets of Systemic Sclerosis.
Anti-Ro (SS-A) antibodies are commonly found in Sjögren syndrome and SLE; while they can occur in other autoimmune diseases, they are not specific for CREST.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1042 (Book Page): About 60% of patients have anticentromere antibodies and this is a biomarker for lcSScl and CREST syndrome.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: Which genetic locus demonstrates the most significant association with the risk of developing Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)?
options: TNF-alpha gene
MHC Class I C1q
IL-23 receptor gene
HLA-DRB1
HLA-C
correctOption: HLA-DRB1
optionExplanations: While TNF-alpha is a key cytokine in RA pathogenesis, polymorphisms in the TNF-alpha gene are not the primary genetic association compared to the MHC region.
C1q deficiency is specifically associated with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) due to defective apoptotic cell clearance, not primarily with RA susceptibility.
IL-23 receptor variants are linked to the spondyloarthritides and Psoriatic Arthritis, but are not the primary susceptibility factor for RA.
The HLA-DRB1 gene, specifically variants at positions 11, 71, and 74 of the DR beta-1 chain, is the most powerful genetic risk factor for RA, often referred to as the shared epitope.
HLA-C is more strongly associated with Psoriatic Arthritis and psoriasis rather than being the primary risk locus for Rheumatoid Arthritis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): The strongest association is with variants in the HLA region and is determined by variations in three amino acids in the HLA-DR β1 molecule (positions 11, 71 and 74)

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: In the immunopathogenesis of RA, what is the role of Citrullination in the development of autoimmunity?
options: It acts as a primary trigger for the hepatic production of acute-phase proteins.
It inhibits the activation of CD4+ T cells by dendritic cells.
It causes direct enzymatic degradation of the articular cartilage matrix.
It modifies host proteins to make them immunogenic in genetically susceptible individuals.
It facilitates the direct infiltration of neutrophils into the synovial fluid.
correctOption: It modifies host proteins to make them immunogenic in genetically susceptible individuals.
optionExplanations: IL-6, not citrullination, is the primary systemic cytokine that travels to the liver to trigger the production of acute-phase reactants like CRP.
Citrullination enhances the presentation of antigens to T cells by modifying peptide binding affinity to the shared epitope, thereby promoting, rather than inhibiting, T cell activation.
Citrullination is a post-translational modification, not a direct proteolytic enzyme that breaks down cartilage like matrix metalloproteinases do.

Citrullination modifies the amino acid arginine to citrulline, which in susceptible hosts (like those with the shared epitope) creates neo-antigens that the immune system recognizes as foreign, leading to ACPA production.
Neutrophil recruitment is driven by chemokines and cytokines like IL-8 and TNF, not by the citrullination process itself.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): It is believed that RA occurs when an environmental stimulus, such as infection, triggers autoimmunity in a genetically susceptible host by modifying host proteins, through processes like citrullination, so that they become immunogenic.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: How does the clinical significance of Anti-Citrullinated Peptide Antibodies (ACPA) differ from Rheumatoid Factor (RF) in the context of RA pathogenesis?
options: RF levels are used specifically to monitor the therapeutic efficacy of IL-6 inhibitors.
ACPA is highly specific for RA and can often be detected before clinical symptoms emerge.
RF is more specific to RA than ACPA.
ACPA is only present in patients with advanced extra-articular disease.
RF is rarely found in other autoimmune or infectious diseases.
correctOption: ACPA is highly specific for RA and can often be detected before clinical symptoms emerge.
optionExplanations: Neither RF nor ACPA levels are primary tools for monitoring therapeutic response to specific biologics; clinical scores like DAS28 are preferred.
ACPA has high specificity and predictive value, often appearing in the serum years before the patient develops clinical synovitis.
ACPA is significantly more specific for RA than RF, which can be found in many other chronic inflammatory conditions.
ACPA is used for diagnosis and classification of early RA, not just in advanced stages of the disease.
Rheumatoid Factor is frequently found in other conditions like Sjögren's syndrome, chronic infections, and even in some healthy elderly individuals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1031 (Book Page): Tests for ACPA are positive in about 70% of cases and are highly specific for RA, occurring in many patients before clinical onset of the disease. Similarly, RF is also positive in about 70% of cases... RF is less specific than ACPA

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: A 58-year-old female with a 15-year history of erosive RA presents to the emergency department with severe occipital headache and sudden-onset 'electric-shock' sensations radiating down both arms when looking down. Physical examination reveals hyperreflexia in the lower limbs. What is the precise pathophysiological cause of this presentation?
options: Development of rheumatoid nodules within the lumbar interspinous ligaments.
Vasculitis of the vasa nervorum causing mononeuritis multiplex.
Degenerative osteophyte formation in the lumbar spine.
Hypertrophied synovium causing compression of the median nerve.
Erosion of the transverse ligament leading to atlanto-axial subluxation.
correctOption: Erosion of the transverse ligament leading to atlanto-axial subluxation.
optionExplanations: Rheumatoid nodules typically occur on extensor surfaces and in internal organs, but do not cause this specific neurological emergency.
Mononeuritis multiplex is a feature of systemic vasculitis and presents with specific motor/sensory deficits in peripheral nerves, not as a central cord syndrome.

While degenerative changes occur, the specific constellation of RA history, occipital headache, and 'electric shocks' in a patient with inflammatory arthritis points strongly to atlanto-axial instability.
Median nerve compression by synovium causes Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, which manifests in the hands, not with occipital headaches and spinal cord signs.

RA often affects the cervical spine. Chronic inflammation can erode the transverse ligament of the atlas, allowing the odontoid peg to compress the spinal cord, especially during flexion (Lhermitte's-like sign).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1031 (Book Page): Atlanto-axial subluxation is due to erosion of the transverse ligament posterior to the odontoid peg. It can lead to cord compression... suspected in any RA patient who describes new onset of occipital headache, particularly if symptoms of paraesthesia or electric shock are present in the arms.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: In the RA inflammatory cascade, which cell-to-cell interaction is responsible for the 'positive feedback loop' that perpetuates chronic synovitis?
options: Dendritic cells suppressing the activation of synovial macrophages.
Synovial macrophages and fibroblasts mutually stimulating each other via TNF-alpha and IL-1.
Neutrophils inhibiting the production of matrix metalloproteinases.
Osteoclast precursors directly activating B cells to produce ACPA.
Plasma cells inducing the production of RANKL by synovial fibroblasts.
correctOption: Synovial macrophages and fibroblasts mutually stimulating each other via TNF-alpha and IL-1.
optionExplanations: Dendritic cells are professional antigen-presenting cells that activate the immune response rather than suppressing synovial macrophages in RA.
This loop is central to RA; macrophages release TNF-alpha/IL-1 which activates fibroblasts to produce more cytokines and degradative enzymes, which in turn further activate macrophages.
Neutrophils in the synovial fluid actually contribute to damage and do not inhibit matrix metalloproteinases.
The activation of B cells is primarily driven by T-cell interactions and cytokines, not by osteoclast precursors.
RANKL is primarily produced by activated T cells and synovial cells to stimulate osteoclasts, not specifically induced by plasma cells in this feedback context.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): The macrophages produce several pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6, which act on synovial fibroblasts to produce further cytokines, setting up a positive feedback loop.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: According to the 2010 EULAR/ACR criteria, what is the minimum duration of symptoms required to contribute a point toward the classification of definite Rheumatoid Arthritis?
options: 6 weeks
12 weeks
6 months
4 weeks
2 weeks
correctOption: 6 weeks
optionExplanations: The criteria assign 1 point if symptoms have persisted for 6 weeks or more, helping to differentiate RA from transient viral arthritides.
12 weeks is not the specific cut-off used in the 2010 classification point system.
6 months is not the threshold; the criteria are designed to facilitate earlier diagnosis, hence the 6-week cut-off.
4 weeks is below the threshold for the chronicity score in the 2010 criteria.
Symptoms lasting only 2 weeks are too acute for the classification of a chronic disease like RA and receive 0 points.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1029 (Book Page): Box 26.52 Criteria for diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis... Duration of symptoms: < 6 weeks (0), > 6 weeks (1).

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: Which mechanism explains the development of the characteristic 'marginal erosions' seen on X-rays of RA patients?
options: Direct pressure from the joint effusion causing bony atrophy.
Crystals of basic calcium phosphate being deposited into the bone.
Osteoclast activation stimulated by RANKL produced by activated T cells.
Bony ankylosis leading to the fusion of the joint space.
Inhibition of M-CSF by synovial macrophages.
correctOption: Osteoclast activation stimulated by RANKL produced by activated T cells.
optionExplanations: Erosions are an active inflammatory and cellular process (pannus invasion), not just a result of physical pressure from fluid.
RA is an inflammatory, non-crystalline arthritis; BCP crystals are associated with osteoarthritis and Milwaukee shoulder.
Activated T cells in the synovium express RANKL, which binds to RANK on osteoclast precursors, triggering their differentiation into mature bone-resorbing cells.
Ankylosis is a late feature representing joint fusion, which is a consequence of the inflammatory process, but does not describe the mechanism of 'erosion' itself.
M-CSF is actually produced by synovial cells to *stimulate* osteoclast precursors, not inhibit them.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): A key pathogenic factor in bone erosions and periarticular osteoporosis is osteoclast activation, stimulated by the production of M-CSF by synovial cells and RANKL by activated T cells.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: A 62-year-old male with active RA presents with sudden, severe pain and swelling in his left calf. He reports that his left knee had been very swollen for several weeks. On examination, the left calf is tender and erythematous. A D-dimer is elevated, but a duplex ultrasound of the deep veins is negative. What is the most likely pathological explanation for this finding?
options: Development of a rheumatoid nodule within the Achilles tendon.
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) that was missed on initial scan.
Rupture of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst.
Spontaneous hematoma due to NSAID-induced coagulopathy.
Infarction of the gastrocnemius muscle due to vasculitis.
correctOption: Rupture of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst.
optionExplanations: Nodules in the Achilles tendon cause localized lumps but do not cause acute calf-wide swelling and erythema mimicking DVT.
The duplex ultrasound is the gold standard; a negative scan in the presence of knee synovitis points more strongly toward cyst rupture.

Knee synovitis in RA leads to high intra-articular pressure, forcing fluid into the popliteal bursa. If this cyst ruptures, synovial fluid tracks down the calf muscles, causing pain and swelling that perfectly mimics DVT (pseudothrombophlebitis).
NSAIDs cause platelet dysfunction, but do not typically cause spontaneous large-scale calf hematomas without trauma.
While RA can cause vasculitis, muscle infarction is much rarer and usually presents with other signs of systemic vasculitis rather than following a period of knee synovitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1029 (Book Page): Popliteal (Baker’s) cysts may occur in patients with knee synovitis... Rupture may be induced by knee flexion, leading to calf pain and swelling that may mimic a deep venous thrombosis (DVT).

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: Which cytokine is the primary driver of the hepatic production of acute-phase proteins (like CRP) and is responsible for systemic features such as weight loss and fatigue in RA?
options: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
Nitric Oxide
Interferon-gamma
Matrix Metalloproteinase-1
ADAMTS-5
correctOption: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
optionExplanations: IL-6 is a pleiotropic cytokine that mediates the systemic inflammatory response in RA, including the liver's production of CRP and the systemic symptoms like fatigue.
Nitric oxide produced in the synovium leads to local vasodilation and pain but is not the driver for hepatic CRP production.
Interferon-gamma is important for activating macrophages but is not the primary cytokine that signals the liver to produce CRP.
Matrix metalloproteinases are enzymes that degrade the extracellular matrix in the joint and do not act as systemic hormones.
ADAMTS-5 is an enzyme (aggrecanase) involved in cartilage breakdown, not a systemic signaling cytokine.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): Systemic release of IL-6 triggers production of acute phase proteins by the liver... Anorexia, weight loss and fatigue may occur throughout the disease course. [Pathophysiology figure 26.33 shows IL-6 leading to Acute phase proteins].

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
statement: Rheumatoid nodules, a common extra-articular feature, are histologically characterized by what structural arrangement?
options: A central area of fibrinoid material surrounded by a palisade of proliferating mononuclear cells.
A collection of monosodium urate crystals.
A cluster of osteoblasts and new bone formation.
A cyst filled with viscous synovial fluid.
A mass of hypertrophied synovial fibroblasts and angiogenesis.
correctOption: A central area of fibrinoid material surrounded by a palisade of proliferating mononuclear cells.
optionExplanations: This is the classic description of a rheumatoid granuloma/nodule, featuring central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a palisade of macrophages/mononuclear cells.
Monosodium urate crystals are characteristic of tophaceous gout, not rheumatoid nodules.
Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells; they are not the primary components of soft-tissue rheumatoid nodules.
A synovial cyst (like a Baker's cyst) is fluid-filled, whereas a rheumatoid nodule is a solid, firm granulomatous structure.
This describes the pannus/synovium itself, not the specific histology of a subcutaneous nodule.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1028 (Book Page): They consist of a central area of fibrinoid material surrounded by a palisade of proliferating mononuclear cells.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
coreConcept: Clinical definition and differentiation of PM vs DM
statement: Which clinical feature fundamentally differentiates the definition of dermatomyositis from polymyositis within the spectrum of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies?
options: Association with underlying occult malignancy
Development of symmetrical proximal muscle weakness
Presence of characteristic cutaneous manifestations
Infiltration of muscle tissue by inflammatory cells
Involvement of the skeletal muscle system
correctOption: Presence of characteristic cutaneous manifestations
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The source text states that both polymyositis and dermatomyositis can occur in association with a previously undiagnosed malignancy, making this a shared risk rather than a definitive differentiator.
Incorrect. Both conditions typically present with the same pattern of symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, usually affecting the lower limbs more significantly than the upper limbs.

Correct. According to the standard clinical definition, dermatomyositis is specifically distinguished from polymyositis by the additional presence of pathognomonic skin lesions, such as Gottron's papules or the heliotrope rash.
Incorrect. An inflammatory infiltrate on muscle biopsy is the pathological hallmark of both conditions, reflecting their shared autoimmune nature, and does not distinguish between the two.
Incorrect. Both polymyositis and dermatomyositis are defined by the inflammatory involvement of skeletal muscle; therefore, muscle involvement is a shared feature rather than a differentiating one.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are characterised by an inflammatory infiltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle. In DM, characteristic skin changes also occur.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
coreConcept: Autoimmune histological basis of inflammatory myopathies
statement: Regarding the histopathological evidence of the autoimmune basis in polymyositis and dermatomyositis, which microscopic triad is considered diagnostic of active immune-mediated injury within the muscle biopsy?
options: Urate crystal deposition, neutrophil activation, and tophi formation
Fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition, and capillary fallout
Adipose tissue replacement, fibre hypertrophy, and absence of nuclei
Fibre necrosis, regeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltrate
Non-caseating granulomas, giant cells, and interstitial edema
correctOption: Fibre necrosis, regeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltrate
optionExplanations: Incorrect. These are the histological features of gout, a metabolic crystalline arthropathy, which is caused by monosodium urate crystals rather than an idiopathic autoimmune attack on muscle fibers.
Incorrect. This description matches the pathological findings of systemic sclerosis (fibrosis and vascular changes) rather than the active inflammatory destruction seen in myositis.

Incorrect. While adipose replacement can occur in end-stage chronic muscle damage (as seen in certain muscular dystrophies), it is not the diagnostic triad for active autoimmune inflammation in PM or DM.

Correct. The autoimmune nature of these diseases is demonstrated on biopsy by the presence of T-lymphocyte-rich inflammatory infiltrates that cause muscle fiber necrosis and trigger reactive fiber regeneration.
Incorrect. Non-caseating granulomas are the hallmark of sarcoidosis. While muscle involvement can occur in sarcoid, it is not the defining feature of PM or DM.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Muscle biopsy is the pivotal investigation and shows the typical features of fibre necrosis, regeneration and inflammatory cell infiltrate.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive, symmetrical weakness in her pelvic and shoulder girdles over the last month. On examination, a distinct violaceous rash is noted on her eyelids accompanied by periorbital edema. Which clinical term specifically defines this cutaneous manifestation characteristic of her condition?
options: Gottron's papules
Heliotrope rash
Livedo reticularis
Erythema nodosum
Shawl sign
correctOption: Heliotrope rash
optionExplanations: Gottron's papules are erythematous or violaceous scaly plaques found specifically over the extensor surfaces of the interphalangeal joints, not the eyelids.
The heliotrope rash is a pathognomonic sign of dermatomyositis, characterized by a violaceous (lilac-colored) eruption on the upper eyelids, often with associated periorbital edema.
Livedo reticularis is a lace-like purplish skin discoloration related to small vessel changes, more common in SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome, not eyelid-specific.
Erythema nodosum consists of painful, red nodules typically on the shins, often associated with Behçet's disease or sarcoidosis, but is not a primary feature of dermatomyositis.
The Shawl sign refers to a diffuse erythematous rash across the upper back, shoulders, and chest, resembling a shawl distribution, rather than the localized eyelid involvement.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): a heliotrope rash that is a violaceous discoloration of the eyelid in combination with periorbital oedema.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: In the pathophysiology of inflammatory myopathies, the presence of antisynthetase antibodies, specifically anti-Jo-1, is a critical immunological marker. These antibodies are most strongly correlated with which intermediate clinical complication involving a non-muscular organ system?
options: Interstitial lung disease
Glomerulonephritis
Aortic regurgitation
Cerebral vasculitis
Mesenteric vasculitis
correctOption: Interstitial lung disease
optionExplanations: The anti-Jo-1 antibody is the most common antisynthetase antibody; its presence defines a subset of patients at high risk for interstitial lung disease (ILD), often manifesting as progressive dyspnea and cough.
Renal involvement like glomerulonephritis is a hallmark of SLE and certain small-vessel vasculitides, but it is extremely rare in isolated polymyositis or dermatomyositis.
Aortic regurgitation is associated with spondyloarthritides like ankylosing spondylitis and occasionally Takayasu arteritis, but not typically with Jo-1 antibodies.
Cerebral vasculitis is a feature of primary CNS vasculitis or severe systemic lupus erythematosus; it is not a recognized component of the Jo-1 antisynthetase syndrome.
Mesenteric vasculitis is a complication of polyarteritis nodosa or systemic lupus erythematosus, involving medium and small arteries of the gut, unlike the pulmonary focus of Jo-1.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Interstitial lung disease occurs in up to 30% of patients and is associated with the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A pivotal diagnostic contrast in the evaluation of myopathy is differentiating inflammatory destruction from non-inflammatory causes. Which histological finding on a muscle biopsy is the definitive indicator of an autoimmune-mediated inflammatory myopathy?
options: Fibre necrosis and regeneration with inflammatory cell infiltrate
Amyloid deposition in vessel walls
Type II fibre atrophy
Widespread fibrinoid necrosis of the media
Adipose tissue replacement without cellular infiltration
correctOption: Fibre necrosis and regeneration with inflammatory cell infiltrate
optionExplanations: The presence of an inflammatory cell infiltrate (typically lymphocytic) alongside evidence of active muscle fibre death (necrosis) and subsequent repair (regeneration) confirms active inflammatory myositis.
Amyloid deposition is the hallmark of systemic amyloidosis, which can cause macroglossia and pseudo-hypertrophy, but not the typical inflammatory infiltrate of PM/DM.
Type II fibre atrophy is a non-specific finding often seen in disuse, chronic illness, or specifically as a side effect of glucocorticoid therapy, rather than primary inflammation.
Fibrinoid necrosis of the media is characteristic of polyarteritis nodosa (vasculitis), affecting the vessel wall rather than the muscle fibres themselves.
Adipose replacement (fatty infiltration) is a late-stage feature of many muscular dystrophies or chronic end-stage myositis, but it lacks the acute cellular inflammation needed for diagnosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Muscle biopsy is the pivotal investigation and shows the typical features of fibre necrosis, regeneration and inflammatory cell infiltrate.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with a three-week history of difficulty rising from his chair and climbing stairs. Examination reveals symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and scaly, violaceous plaques over his metacarpophalangeal joints. Given his age and clinical presentation, which clinical strategy is prioritized after confirming the diagnosis of dermatomyositis?
options: Screening for HLA-B27 positivity
Long-term prophylactic anticoagulation
Assessment for human parvovirus B19 IgM
Immediate search for an underlying malignancy
High-dose penicillin for rheumatic fever
correctOption: Immediate search for an underlying malignancy
optionExplanations: HLA-B27 is associated with the spondyloarthritides (like ankylosing spondylitis), not the inflammatory myopathies polymyositis or dermatomyositis.
Anticoagulation is indicated in antiphospholipid syndrome but is not a routine requirement for the management of dermatomyositis unless a specific thrombotic event occurs.
Parvovirus B19 typically causes a self-limiting polyarthritis in adults (slapped cheek in children), not a necrotizing proximal myopathy with Gottron's papules.
In adults, especially those over 40, dermatomyositis and polymyositis are frequently paraneoplastic syndromes. A comprehensive cancer screen (CT, mammography, PSA) is mandatory at diagnosis.
Penicillin is used for rheumatic fever to treat streptococcal infections; however, dermatomyositis is an autoimmune myopathy, not a post-streptococcal disease.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Both diseases are rare... they can occur in isolation or in association with other autoimmune diseases and both may be the presenting features of a previously undiagnosed malignancy.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A patient with polymyositis has been treated with prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) for four months. While his serum creatine kinase (CK) has normalized, he reports a new, progressive weakness in his lower limbs. A repeat biopsy is performed. Which histological finding would confirm a glucocorticoid-induced myopathy rather than an inflammatory relapse?
options: Fibrinoid necrosis of the endomysial capillaries
Extensive lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate
Basophilic stippling of the sarcoplasm
Type II fibre atrophy
Widespread fibre necrosis and regeneration
correctOption: Type II fibre atrophy
optionExplanations: Fibrinoid necrosis is a vascular lesion seen in vasculitis and is not a feature of either steroid myopathy or primary polymyositis.
An extensive inflammatory infiltrate would indicate that the original autoimmune process (polymyositis) is still active or relapsing, not a drug side effect.
Basophilic stippling is more commonly associated with lead poisoning in red blood cells; it is not a diagnostic marker for steroid-induced muscle damage.
Long-term or high-dose glucocorticoids cause a non-inflammatory myopathy characterized histologically by the selective atrophy of Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibres.
Fibre necrosis and regeneration are hallmarks of active inflammatory myositis; their absence with normalized CK suggests the inflammation is controlled.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): in the case of glucocorticoid myopathy type II fibre atrophy is observed as compared with fibre necrosis and regeneration in active myositis.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: According to standard clinical descriptions, which of the following best characterizes the typical distribution and onset of muscle involvement in polymyositis?
options: Unilateral weakness of the facial muscles
Symmetrical proximal weakness of the lower and upper limbs
Asymmetrical pelvic girdle weakness with preserved shoulder function
Symmetrical distal weakness of the feet
Asymmetrical distal weakness of the hands
correctOption: Symmetrical proximal weakness of the lower and upper limbs
optionExplanations: Facial muscle involvement is rare in polymyositis and would suggest other neurological conditions like Myasthenia Gravis or Bell's palsy.
Polymyositis typically presents as a subacute, symmetrical weakness of the proximal muscle groups, making tasks like rising from a chair or lifting objects difficult.
While the lower limbs (pelvic girdle) are often more affected, the weakness in PM is characteristically symmetrical and usually involves the shoulder girdle as well.
Distal weakness of the feet (e.g., foot drop) is suggestive of a peripheral nerve lesion or a distal myopathy, not the proximal girdle involvement of PM.
Distal weakness is more characteristic of neuropathies or inclusion body myositis, whereas polymyositis classically affects the proximal musculature.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): The typical presentation of PM and DM is with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness over a few weeks, usually affecting the lower limbs more than the upper

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: Muscle involvement in inflammatory myopathies can be patchy, potentially leading to false-negative results during a blind biopsy. To identify the most active areas of inflammation and increase diagnostic yield, which imaging modality and sequence is recommended?
options: CT scan with bone window
Doppler ultrasound of the temporal artery
Plain X-ray of the long bones
Technetium-99m bone scan
MRI with STIR sequence
correctOption: MRI with STIR sequence
optionExplanations: CT scans are excellent for evaluating bone architecture and calcification but lack the soft tissue resolution to identify subtle muscular inflammation.
Temporal artery Doppler is used in the diagnosis of Giant Cell Arteritis (the 'halo sign'), not for evaluating skeletal muscle in polymyositis.
Plain X-rays are useful for detecting end-stage joint damage or fractures but cannot visualize the inflammatory process within the muscle tissue.
Bone scans identify areas of increased bone turnover (osteoblastic activity) and are not utilized for the primary diagnosis of inflammatory myositis.
Short Tau Inversion Recovery (STIR) MRI sequences are highly sensitive to oedema; increased signal in muscle tissue indicates active inflammation, guiding the biopsy to that specific site.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Since muscle involvement may be patchy, it is common to perform an MRI scan prior to biopsy, which often shows features of increased signal intensity in STIR sequence images.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 7-year-old girl presents with a purple-red rash on her eyelids and scaly plaques on her knuckles. She has developed significant difficulty walking and climbing stairs over the past month. Which statement correctly distinguishes the management or prognosis of her condition from the adult form of the disease?
options: Calcinosis occurs in less than 1% of children with this condition.
Glucocorticoids are strictly contraindicated in her age group.
She requires urgent screening for an occult visceral malignancy.
Her condition typically does not require a search for malignancy.
The condition is always monocyclic and resolves within six months.
correctOption: Her condition typically does not require a search for malignancy.
optionExplanations: Calcinosis (subcutaneous calcification) is actually more common in children, occurring in approximately 30% of JDM cases, compared to fewer adults.
Glucocorticoids (often starting with IV methylprednisolone) are actually the first-line treatment for JDM to achieve rapid control of inflammation.
Unlike adult dermatomyositis, the juvenile form (JDM) is rarely associated with malignancy; therefore, intensive cancer screening is not standard for children.
JDM is the most common pediatric inflammatory myopathy. It is distinct from the adult version primarily because it lacks the strong association with paraneoplastic syndromes.
JDM has several courses; 60-75% of cases are polycyclic (relapsing and remitting) or chronic, rather than purely monocyclic and brief.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is by far the most common inflammatory myopathy in children and adolescents, and typically does not require a search for malignancy.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: In the clinical regulation and monitoring of a patient diagnosed with dermatomyositis, which biochemical laboratory parameter serves as the primary measure for assessing the intensity of active muscle damage and the response to therapy?
options: Serum Uric Acid
Serum Creatine Kinase (CK)
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
Serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
correctOption: Serum Creatine Kinase (CK)
optionExplanations: Serum uric acid is a marker for gout and hyperuricemia; it does not reflect the degree of skeletal muscle inflammation or necrosis.

Creatine Kinase (CK) is an enzyme found inside muscle cells; when the cell membrane is damaged by autoimmune inflammation (necrotizing myositis), CK leaks into the serum, making its level a direct correlate of muscle damage.
ESR is a non-specific marker of the acute phase response; while it may be elevated, it does not provide the tissue-specific information that CK does for myositis.
Alkaline Phosphatase is primarily a marker of bone turnover or cholestatic liver disease; it is not elevated as a direct result of muscle fibre necrosis.
While CRP can be elevated in systemic inflammation, it is often normal in active SLE or purely localized muscle disease; it is not the primary marker for muscle destruction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Serum levels of creatine kinase are typically raised and are a useful measure of disease activity

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: Dermatomyositis often presents with characteristic psoriasiform plaques known as Gottron’s papules. These are classically found over the extensor surfaces of which specific joints?
options: Atlanto-axial joints
Sacroiliac (SI) joints
Temporomandibular joints
Distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP/PIP) joints
Metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints
correctOption: Distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP/PIP) joints
optionExplanations: The atlanto-axial joint is in the cervical spine; its subluxation is a serious complication of Rheumatoid Arthritis, not a site for the cutaneous markers of DM.
Sacroiliac joints are involved in axial spondyloarthritis; they are deep internal joints and do not manifest with superficial papules like the PIP/DIP joints.
The temporomandibular joint is involved in chewing; while jaw claudication can occur in Giant Cell Arteritis, it is not a site for Gottron's papules.
Gottron's papules are a hallmark cutaneous sign of dermatomyositis, localized to the extensor (dorsal) aspects of the PIP and DIP joints of the fingers.
MTP joints are located in the feet and are the primary site for Podagra in gout, but they are not the typical location for Gottron's papules.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Gottron’s papules, which are scaly, erythematous or violaceous, psoriasiform plaques occurring over the extensor surfaces of PIP and DIP joints

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
coreConcept: Definition and Pathological Basis of Myositis
statement: Which of the following pathological featur es fundamentally defines both polymyositis and dermatomyositis within the spectrum of autoimmune connective tissue diseases?
options: Primary degeneration of the neuromuscular junction without cellular infiltration
Deposition of monosodium urate crystals within the myofibrils
Non-inflammatory accumulation of glycogen within the sarcoplasm of type I fibres
Widespread vasculitis of the large-sized elastic arteries only
Inammatory inltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle
correctOption: Inammatory inltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle
optionExplanations: Degeneration of the neuromuscular junction without infiltration is characteristic of Myasthenia Gravis (an antibody-mediated blockade) or Eaton-Lambert syndrome, not PM/DM which are inflammatory and infiltrative cell-mediated processes at the muscle fibre level/vasculature level (DM).
Monosodium urate crystal deposition is the hallmark of gout, a crystal-induced arthropathy, and does not occur within the myofibrils in autoimmune myositis.
Non-inflammatory glycogen accumulation is characteristic of metabolic storage myopathies, such as Pompe disease, not autoimmune inflammatory myopathies like PM or DM.

While DM involves small-vessel changes, the fundamental definition focuses on muscle infiltration; large-vessel vasculitis is characteristic of conditions like Giant Cell Arteritis or Takayasu Arteritis.
PM and DM are defined by an autoimmune-mediated inflammatory process where leukocytes (lymphocytes and macrophages) infiltrate muscle tissue, leading to fibre damage and clinical weakness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are characterised by an inflammatory infiltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 52-year-old male is undergoing evaluation for suspected polymyositis. In the context of this autoimmune condition, what is the specific mechanistic significance of using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) with Short T1 Inversion Recovery (STIR) sequences?
options: It provides a definitive histopathological diagnosis by visualising inflammatory cells at the molecular level
It confirms the presence of subungual hyperkeratosis which is pathognomonic for PM
It identifies areas of chronic fatty replacement which are the primary sites for biopsy
It differentiates between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle involvement in the upper limbs
It demonstrates increased signal intensity reflecting active inflammatory oedema to guide biopsy
correctOption: It demonstrates increased signal intensity reflecting active inflammatory oedema to guide biopsy
optionExplanations: MRI provides imaging evidence of oedema/inflammation but cannot provide 'definitive histopathological' diagnosis; only a tissue biopsy and microscopic examination can do that.
Subungual hyperkeratosis is a clinical skin finding in DM/gout/psoriasis, not a finding evaluated by muscle MRI, and is not pathognomonic for PM.
Fatty replacement indicates chronic, end-stage damage; a biopsy of such tissue would be non-diagnostic (showing only fibrosis) rather than active inflammation.
While both may be involved, MRI's primary clinical role in this context is locating active skeletal muscle inflammation to avoid biopsy errors, not specifically differentiating smooth muscle layers.
Active autoimmune inflammation in PM/DM causes muscle oedema, which appears as hyperintensity on STIR MRI. Since the disease is patchy, MRI identifies the 'hottest' spots for a high-yield biopsy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): since muscle involvement may be patchy, it is common to perform an MRI scan prior to biopsy, which often shows features of increased signal intensity in STIR sequence images. This not only provides support for the diagnosis, but also can help choose the optimal site for a biopsy.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: When contrasting the systemic complications of autoimmune myositis, the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies is most specifically associated with which clinical manifestation?
options: Isolated malar facial rash sparing the nasolabial folds
Interstitial lung disease
Progressive atlanto-axial subluxation with spinal cord compression
Antral vascular ectasia (watermelon stomach)
Primary biliary cholangitis
correctOption: Interstitial lung disease
optionExplanations: Malar rashes are classically associated with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), not specifically the Jo-1 antibody in myositis.

The Jo-1 antibody is the most common antisynthetase antibody and is a marker for 'Antisynthetase Syndrome', which characteristically includes interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's, and 'mechanic's hands'.
Atlanto-axial subluxation is a serious complication of Rheumatoid Arthritis due to erosion of the transverse ligament, not PM/DM.
Watermelon stomach is an occasional gastrointestinal manifestation of Systemic Sclerosis, not a core feature of Jo-1 positive myositis.
Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune liver disease that may coexist with Sjogren's syndrome but is not the primary association for the Jo-1 antibody.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Interstitial lung disease occurs in up to 30% of patients and is associated with the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with a 4-week history of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from her chair. On examination, she has violaceous discoloration of her eyelids and scaly, violaceous plaques over her proximal interphalangeal joints. Her vitals show a heart rate of 92 bpm, blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 28 bpm with shallow breathing. She reports difficulty swallowing liquids. What is the most immediate clinical priority for this patient based on her presentation?
options: Assessment of pharyngeal and respiratory muscle involvement to prevent failure
Application of topical glucocorticoids to the Gottron's papules
Scheduling a muscle biopsy of the gastrocnemius muscle without prior imaging
Routine screening for underlying colorectal malignancy via colonoscopy
Initiation of high-dose oral hydroxychloroquine for the skin lesions
correctOption: Assessment of pharyngeal and respiratory muscle involvement to prevent failure
optionExplanations: In DM/PM, involvement of the pharyngeal muscles (causing dysphagia/aspiration) and respiratory muscles (causing ventilatory failure) is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate stabilization.
Topical steroids treat local skin symptoms but do not address the systemic autoimmune process or the life-threatening muscle weakness affecting breathing and swallowing.
Biopsy is important for diagnosis, but clinical stabilization and checking respiratory function (e.g., FVC) must come first; additionally, MRI is usually preferred to guide the biopsy site.
While malignancy screening is essential in adult-onset DM, it is not the 'most immediate' priority for a patient in potential respiratory distress.
Hydroxychloroquine may be used for skin-predominant disease, but it is not the priority when the patient has signs of respiratory distress (RR 28) and dysphagia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Respiratory or pharyngeal muscle involvement can lead to ventilatory failure or aspiration that requires urgent treatment.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: In a patient initially treated for polymyositis who experiences a relapse of muscle weakness after several months of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy, what histopathological finding on a second muscle biopsy would most strongly suggest glucocorticoid-induced myopathy rather than active myositis?
options: Abundant IgG4-secreting plasma cells
Type II fibre atrophy
Fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles with ANCA positivity
Focal lymphocytic infiltration in the perichondrium
Intense inflammatory cell infiltrate with areas of fibre necrosis
correctOption: Type II fibre atrophy
optionExplanations: IgG4-secreting plasma cells define IgG4-related disease, which can involve salivary glands or the retroperitoneum, but is not a feature of steroid-induced muscle damage.
Long-term glucocorticoid use causes selective atrophy of Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibres without an inflammatory infiltrate. This distinguishes drug-induced weakness from an autoimmune flare.
Fibrinoid necrosis with ANCA is characteristic of ANCA-associated vasculitis (like GPA or MPA), which is a different autoimmune pathology entirely.
Lymphocytic infiltration in the perichondrium is the diagnostic feature of Relapsing Polychondritis, not myositis or steroid myopathy.
Inflammatory infiltrates and fibre necrosis are the hallmarks of the original autoimmune disease (active myositis), indicating a failure of treatment or a true disease flare.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): A second muscle biopsy can be of diagnostic value... since in the case of glucocorticoid myopathy type II fibre atrophy is observed as compared with fibre necrosis and regeneration in active myositis.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: What is the reported annual incidence range for both polymyositis and dermatomyositis in the general population?
options: 2–10 per million
correctOption: 2–10 per million
optionExplanations: 10–20 per 100,000 is the prevalence of Systemic Sclerosis, not the annual incidence of PM/DM.
2–10 per 100,000 is the reported incidence for Septic Arthritis in the general population, not PM/DM.
1–2 per 1,000 (0.1-0.2%) is more typical of commoner autoimmune conditions like Rheumatoid Arthritis in some populations, but far too high for PM/DM.
PM and DM are categorized as rare autoimmune diseases, with a very low incidence of 2 to 10 cases per million per year.
30–70 per 100,000 is the incidence of Septic Arthritis in patients with pre-existing joint disease or prosthetics.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Both diseases are rare, with an incidence of 2–10 cases per million/year.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A clinician is evaluating a 55-year-old female for dermatomyositis. To fulfill the standard workup for an adult with this autoimmune diagnosis, which of the following is mandatory to exclude a common associated condition?
options: Screening for underlying malignancy via full examination and CT imaging
Conducting a pathergy test to check for pustule development
Evaluating for Schirmer tear test and minor salivary gland biopsy
Performing a distal finger tingling test for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Testing for HLA-B27 and sacroiliac joint imaging
correctOption: Screening for underlying malignancy via full examination and CT imaging
optionExplanations: Adult-onset DM is frequently a paraneoplastic syndrome. Autoimmune mechanisms are triggered by the tumor, making routine malignancy screening mandatory for these patients.
The pathergy test is specific for Behçet’s disease, an autoimmune vasculitis, not dermatomyositis.
Schirmer test and salivary gland biopsy are used to diagnose Sjogren's syndrome, which can coexist with other AICTDs but isn't the primary 'mandatory' exclusion in new-onset DM.
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is a compression neuropathy common in RA or SSc, but its assessment is not a mandatory part of the standard DM diagnostic workup.
HLA-B27 is associated with Spondyloarthritides (like Ankylosing Spondylitis), not specifically PM/DM.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): both may be the presenting features of a previously undiagnosed malignancy... Screening for underlying malignancy should be undertaken routinely (full examination, chest X-ray, serum urine and protein electrophoresis, CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis; prostate-specific antigen in men and mammography in women).

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with symmetrical weakness of the quadriceps and deltoids. He has scaly, violaceous plaques on his knuckles and a violaceous rash on his eyelids. Investigations reveal a Creatine Kinase of 4,500 U/L (Normal <170). A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a large mass in the head of the pancreas with local lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely autoimmune classification of his muscle disease?
options: Inclusion Body Myositis secondary to Hepatitis C
Staphylococcal Pyomyositis
Paraneoplastic Dermatomyositis
Mixed Connective Tissue Disease with anti-RNP antibodies
Primary Juvenile Dermatomyositis
correctOption: Paraneoplastic Dermatomyositis
optionExplanations: Inclusion body myositis typically involves distal muscles (flexors of fingers) and is less associated with the classic violaceous rashes of DM.
Pyomyositis is a bacterial infection (usually Staph) of the muscle, typically presenting with localized pain, fever, and pus, not the symmetrical autoimmune rashes of DM.

The clinical signs (Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, proximal weakness) and the presence of a pancreatic mass strongly indicate dermatomyositis occurring as a paraneoplastic manifestation of an underlying cancer.
MCTD involves features of SLE, Scleroderma, and Myositis together, but the specific pancreatic finding and classic DM skin signs point directly to a paraneoplastic DM.
Juvenile DM occurs in children/adolescents (median age 7) and typically does NOT require a search for malignancy, unlike this 58-year-old patient.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): characteristically skin changes also occur... both may be the presenting features of a previously undiagnosed malignancy.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: The autoimmune skin lesion described as 'scaly, erythematous or violaceous, psoriasiform plaques occurring over the extensor surfaces of PIP and DIP joints' in dermatomyositis is known as:
options: Livedo reticularis
Circinate balanitis
Heliotrope rash
Keratoderma blennorrhagica
Gottron's papules
correctOption: Gottron's papules
optionExplanations: Livedo reticularis is a lace-like purplish skin discoloration seen in SLE, Antiphospholipid Syndrome, or Vasculitis, not localized to knuckles.
Circinate balanitis is a skin feature of Reactive Arthritis, occurring on the glans penis.
Heliotrope rash is a violaceous discoloration of the eyelids specifically, often with periorbital edema.
Keratoderma blennorrhagica refers to crusty plaques on the palms and soles, also characteristic of Reactive Arthritis.
Gottron's papules are pathognomonic skin features of DM located over the small joints of the hands.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): The skin lesions in DM include Gottron’s papules, which are scaly, erythematous or violaceous, psoriasiform plaques occurring over the extensor surfaces of PIP and DIP joints

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: Which biochemical laboratory marker is typically elevated in the early, active phase of autoimmune inflammatory myopathy and serves as a useful measure of disease activity?
options: Serum uric acid
Alkaline phosphatase
Creatine kinase
C-reactive protein
Alpha-fetoprotein
correctOption: Creatine kinase
optionExplanations: Serum uric acid is used to monitor gout; its elevation is related to purine metabolism, not inflammatory muscle destruction.
Alkaline phosphatase is a marker of bone turnover or cholestasis, not primary muscle inflammation.
Creatine kinase (CK) is released from damaged muscle fibres. In active autoimmune myositis, high levels reflect the degree of ongoing muscle fibre necrosis.
While CRP can be raised in many inflammatory states, it is non-specific; CK is the more specific marker for muscle tissue damage in PM/DM.
Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumor marker (e.g., for hepatocellular carcinoma), not a marker of autoimmune muscle inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): Serum levels of creatine kinase are typically raised and are a useful measure of disease activity, although a normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
coreConcept: Definition and Tissue Targets of Polymyositis
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with progressive difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing stairs over the past month. Clinical evaluation reveals symmetrical proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory analysis confirms an inflammatory infiltrate involving both skeletal and smooth muscle. Based on the fundamental pathological definition, which condition is most likely?
options: Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Myasthenia gravis
Polymyositis
Fibromyalgia
Inclusion body myositis
correctOption: Polymyositis
optionExplanations: Lambert-Eaton syndrome is a presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission usually associated with small cell lung cancer, not primary muscle inflammation.
Myasthenia gravis is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction caused by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, not an inflammatory infiltrate of the muscle itself.
Polymyositis is defined by an autoimmune-mediated inflammatory infiltrate affecting the skeletal and smooth muscles, typically presenting with proximal weakness.
Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome characterized by widespread pain and tender points without objective muscle inflammation or weakness.
Inclusion body myositis is a distinct inflammatory myopathy often affecting distal muscles and showing specific vacuoles on biopsy, unlike the classic PM infiltrate.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1042 (Book Page): Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are characterised by an inflammatory infiltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A patient diagnosed with an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy is found to have positive antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies. Which specific pathophysiological complication is most strongly associated with this autoimmune marker?
options: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Primary biliary cholangitis
Interstitial lung disease
Mitral valve prolapse
correctOption: Interstitial lung disease
optionExplanations: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis, not typically seen as a primary feature of PM/DM.
While PM/DM can be paraneoplastic, there is no specific association between Jo-1 antibodies and hepatocellular carcinoma in the source text.
Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune liver disease associated with antimitochondrial antibodies, not Jo-1 antibodies.
In approximately 30% of PM/DM cases, the autoimmune process targets the lungs, leading to interstitial lung disease, particularly in Jo-1 positive patients.
Valvular heart disease like mitral valve prolapse is not a recognized autoimmune manifestation of the antisynthetase syndrome described in the text.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Interstitial lung disease occurs in up to 30% of patients and is associated with the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: When differentiating dermatomyositis from polymyositis, which clinical finding serves as the defining diagnostic contrast between these two rare inflammatory conditions?
options: Elevated serum creatine kinase levels
Characteristic cutaneous eruptions
Excellent response to glucocorticoids
Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness
Inflammatory infiltration on muscle biopsy
correctOption: Characteristic cutaneous eruptions
optionExplanations: Creatine kinase (CK) is elevated in both PM and DM due to muscle fiber damage and inflammation, thus it is not a differentiating factor.
The presence of specific skin manifestations, such as Gottron's papules or a heliotrope rash, is the primary feature that distinguishes DM from PM.
Glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment for both conditions; therefore, the treatment response does not help in differentiating the diagnosis.
Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness is a shared hallmark of both conditions and cannot be used to differentiate them.
Both conditions show inflammatory cell infiltrates on muscle biopsy, though the specific location of the infiltrate (perifascicular vs endomysial) may differ.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1042 (Book Page): In DM, characteristic skin changes also occur. . . Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are characterised by an inflammatory infiltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with a two-month history of progressive weakness in his hips and shoulders. On examination, he has violaceous discoloration of the eyelids and scaly erythematous plaques over his PIP joints. Laboratory tests show a CK of 4,000 U/L. Which immediate diagnostic strategy is most critical for this patient based on his clinical presentation?
options: Starting long-term antibiotic prophylaxis
Urgent referral for a renal biopsy
Comprehensive screening for underlying malignancy
Initiating high-dose aspirin therapy
Conducting a pathergy skin test
correctOption: Comprehensive screening for underlying malignancy
optionExplanations: PM and DM are autoimmune, not infectious; antibiotics have no role in the primary management or diagnostic workup.
Renal involvement is not a primary feature of DM; therefore, a renal biopsy is not indicated as an immediate diagnostic priority.
In adults aged 40-60, DM/PM can be the presenting feature of an occult malignancy, requiring comprehensive screening including CT and organ-specific tests.
High-dose aspirin is used in Kawasaki disease or as an antiplatelet, but the primary treatment for DM is glucocorticoids, not aspirin.
The pathergy test is used specifically for the diagnosis of Behçet’s disease, not for inflammatory myopathies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Screening for underlying malignancy should be undertaken routinely (full examination, chest X-ray, serum urine and protein electrophoresis, CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis; prostate-specific antigen in men and mammography in women).

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A patient with long-standing polymyositis on high-dose prednisolone reports worsening leg weakness despite a recent decrease in his serum creatine kinase levels. What histological finding on a second muscle biopsy would confirm glucocorticoid-induced myopathy rather than a disease relapse?
options: Type II fibre atrophy
Enlarged and tortuous nail-fold capillaries
Fibre necrosis and regeneration
Subcutaneous calcification
Dense lymphocytic infiltrate
correctOption: Type II fibre atrophy
optionExplanations: Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy is characterized by selective atrophy of type II muscle fibers without active inflammatory infiltrates.
Nail-fold capillary changes are a clinical sign of dermatomyositis, not a histological feature of steroid-induced muscle damage.
Fibre necrosis and regeneration are hallmarks of active inflammatory myositis (relapse), which would be absent in steroid-induced myopathy.
Subcutaneous calcification (calcinosis) is a complication of chronic DM/PM, especially in juveniles, not a sign of steroid myopathy.
A dense lymphocytic infiltrate indicates ongoing autoimmune activity and would point toward a relapse of the primary polymyositis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): A second muscle biopsy can be of diagnostic value to guide further treatment in this situation since in the case of glucocorticoid myopathy type II fibre atrophy is observed as compared with fibre necrosis and regeneration in active myositis.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: In the clinical evaluation of a suspected case of dermatomyositis, scaly erythematous plaques are specifically noted over the extensor surfaces of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. What is the medical term for these autoimmune-mediated skin lesions?
options: Gottron's papules
Janeway lesions
Livedo reticularis
Heliotrope rash
Malar rash
correctOption: Gottron's papules
optionExplanations: Gottron's papules are pathognomonic scaly plaques found over the finger joints in patients with dermatomyositis.
Janeway lesions are non-tender macules on the palms and soles associated with infective endocarditis, not dermatomyositis.
Livedo reticularis is a lace-like purplish skin pattern seen in SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome, not classic for DM.
Heliotrope rash refers specifically to the violaceous discoloration and edema of the eyelids in dermatomyositis.
A malar rash is a fixed erythema over the cheeks typically sparing the nasolabial folds, characteristic of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Gottron’s papules, which are scaly, erythematous or violaceous, psoriasiform plaques occurring over the extensor surfaces of PIP and DIP joints

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: An elite examiner utilizes Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to evaluate a patient with suspected polymyositis. What specific finding on the STIR sequence images would guide the clinician to the optimal site for a muscle biopsy?
options: Bony erosions at tendon insertions
Fatty replacement of muscle fibers
Punched-out cortical lesions
Increased signal intensity
Vessel wall thickening and necrosis
correctOption: Increased signal intensity
optionExplanations: Bony erosions are features of inflammatory arthritis (like RA or PsA), not the muscle inflammation characteristic of PM.
Fatty replacement of muscle indicates chronic, end-stage damage rather than the active inflammation needed for a diagnostic biopsy.
Punched-out lesions are typically found on X-rays in chronic gout (tophi) or multiple myeloma, not on MRI for polymyositis.
Increased signal intensity on STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) sequences represents edema and active inflammation, highlighting the best muscle for biopsy.
Vessel wall thickening and necrosis are features of vasculitis, which is distinct from the primary interstitial muscle inflammation in PM.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): it is common to perform an MRI scan prior to biopsy, which often shows features of increased signal intensity in STIR sequence images. This not only provides support for the diagnosis, but also can help choose the optimal site for a biopsy.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A 7-year-old child presents with proximal muscle weakness and a violaceous eyelid rash. The child is diagnosed with juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM). Compared to the adult-onset form of the disease, which feature is uniquely observed or more frequent in this pediatric presentation?
options: Subcutaneous calcinosis in 30% of cases
Absence of any skin manifestations
Strong association with occult malignancy
Universal presence of anti-Ro antibodies
Primary involvement of distal muscle groups
correctOption: Subcutaneous calcinosis in 30% of cases
optionExplanations: Calcinosis (subcutaneous calcium deposits) is much more common in JDM, occurring in about 30% of patients, often leading to skin ulceration.
Dermatomyositis, by definition (both juvenile and adult), must include characteristic skin changes; an 'absence' would suggest PM.
Unlike adult-onset DM, juvenile dermatomyositis typically does not require an extensive search for malignancy as the association is extremely rare.
The source text mentions Jo-1 antibodies for PM/DM in general but does not state that anti-Ro antibodies are universally present in JDM.
JDM, like the adult form, primarily affects proximal muscle groups (rising from chairs, climbing stairs), not distal muscles.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM). . . typically does not require a search for malignancy. . . Skin ulceration occurs in 10%–20% of cases and calcinosis in about 30%.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A clinician monitors a patient with dermatomyositis who is undergoing glucocorticoid therapy. Which laboratory marker, often significantly elevated at diagnosis, is used as a serial measure to track disease activity and response to treatment?
options: Serum creatine kinase
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Alkaline phosphatase
Serum albumin levels
Antinuclear antibody titre
correctOption: Serum creatine kinase
optionExplanations: Creatine kinase (CK) levels reflect the degree of muscle fiber breakdown and are generally used to monitor response to therapy in PM/DM.
ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation; while it may be raised, the source identifies CK as the specific measure for muscle disease activity.
Alkaline phosphatase is primarily a marker of bone turnover or biliary stasis and is not used to monitor inflammatory muscle disease.
Serum albumin is a marker of nutrition and chronic inflammation (negative acute phase reactant) but does not specifically track myositis activity.
ANA titers often remain positive regardless of clinical disease activity and are not used for serial monitoring of treatment response.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Serum levels of creatine kinase are typically raised and are a useful measure of disease activity, although a normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: Regarding the epidemiological profile of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, which peak age range and incidence are most accurate for adult polymyositis and dermatomyositis?
options: Age 70–80 years; 2–10 cases per million/year
Age 10–15 years; 50 cases per million/year
Age 40–60 years; 2–10 cases per million/year
Age 40–60 years; 1% of the general population
Age 20–30 years; 100 cases per million/year
correctOption: Age 40–60 years; 2–10 cases per million/year
optionExplanations: While it can occur in older patients, the peak age of onset is 40-60, not 70-80 years.
The 10-15 age group would categorize cases as juvenile myositis, and the incidence is incorrectly high.
Adult PM and DM are rare conditions peaking in the 40-60 age group with an incidence of approximately 2 to 10 cases per million annually.
The incidence is cases per million, not 1% (which would be 10,000 cases per million), as PM and DM are considered rare diseases.
The 20-30 age group is typical for SLE, and the incidence provided here is far too high for inflammatory myopathies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page): Both diseases are rare, with an incidence of 2–10 cases per million/year. . . The typical presentation of PM and DM is with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness. . . in adults between 40 and 60 years of age.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: Which of the following is the hallmark clinical presentation characteristic of both polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM)?
options: Asymmetrical distal muscle weakness and atrophy
Widespread musculoskeletal pain without weakness
Primary involvement of the facial and extraocular muscles
Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness
Small joint erosive polyarthritis
correctOption: Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness
optionExplanations: Asymmetrical distal weakness is more characteristic of inclusion body myositis or neurological conditions like ALS, whereas PM/DM typically present symmetrically and proximally.
Widespread pain without objective weakness is the defining feature of fibromyalgia, not the inflammatory myopathies which are defined by muscle weakness rather than pain.

Involvement of facial and extraocular muscles is very rare in PM/DM and should instead prompt an evaluation for myasthenia gravis or muscular dystrophies if present early in the disease course as primary symptoms according to the text context on mimicry (page 1105). Oral/pharyngeal muscles may be involved late, but not primary extraocular muscles as a rule for these diseases (page 1102).
The hallmark of inflammatory myopathies like PM and DM is symmetrical proximal weakness, classically causing difficulty with tasks such as rising from a chair or climbing stairs.
Small joint erosive polyarthritis is the characteristic feature of Rheumatoid Arthritis; joint involvement in PM/DM is usually non-erosive arthralgia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page) / 1428: The typical presentation of PM and DM is with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness over a few weeks, usually affecting the lower limbs more than the upper, in adults between 40 and 60 years of age.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: In the autoimmune pathogenesis of polymyositis (PM), which pathological mechanism is primarily responsible for the destruction of skeletal muscle fibers?
options: IgA-mediated immune complex deposition in the vessel walls
Type I collagen overproduction by activated fibroblasts
Inflammatory infiltration of skeletal and smooth muscle by lymphocytes
Deposition of urate crystals within the muscle sarcoplasm
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody-mediated necrosis
correctOption: Inflammatory infiltration of skeletal and smooth muscle by lymphocytes
optionExplanations: IgA-mediated deposition is the mechanism for Henoch-Schönlein purpura, not PM. PM is characterized by direct cellular infiltration rather than vasculitic IgA complexes.
Activated fibroblasts and type I collagen overproduction are the primary drivers of fibrosis in systemic sclerosis, not the primary mechanism of muscle fiber destruction in PM.
The primary autoimmune driver in PM is the infiltration of muscle tissue by inflammatory cells, specifically lymphocytes, leading to fiber necrosis and subsequent regeneration as seen on biopsy.
Urate crystal deposition is the hallmark of gout. While crystals can deposit in soft tissues, they are not the pathophysiological mechanism for PM.
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (ACPA) antibodies are specific for Rheumatoid Arthritis and do not play a known role in the necrosis of muscle fibers in polymyositis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page) / 1428: Polymyositis (PM) and dermatomyositis (DM) are characterised by an inflammatory infiltrate of both skeletal and smooth muscle.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: A patient with established polymyositis on high-dose prednisolone reports worsening muscle weakness. Which biopsy finding would most accurately differentiate glucocorticoid-induced myopathy from a flare of active inflammatory myositis?
options: Presence of Gottron's papules on histologic cross-section
Extensive fiber necrosis and regeneration
Type II fiber atrophy in the absence of inflammation
Subcutaneous calcification and skin ulceration
Focal lymphocytic infiltration in the perimysium
correctOption: Type II fiber atrophy in the absence of inflammation
optionExplanations: Gottron's papules are clinical skin lesions found in dermatomyositis, not a microscopic biopsy finding used to differentiate types of myopathy.
Fiber necrosis and regeneration are hallmarks of active myositis. If these are present, it suggests the disease is not adequately controlled rather than being a steroid side effect.

Type II fiber atrophy is the specific histopathological signature of glucocorticoid-induced myopathy. Its presence without inflammatory necrosis points toward drug toxicity rather than disease activity.

Calcification and ulceration are complications of chronic dermatomyositis or polymyositis (calcinosis cutis), but they do not help differentiate the cause of new-onset muscle weakness between steroids and inflammation.
Lymphocytic infiltration is a marker of active inflammatory myositis, whereas steroid myopathy is non-inflammatory.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page) / 1428: A second muscle biopsy can be of diagnostic value to guide further treatment in this situation since in the case of glucocorticoid myopathy type II fibre atrophy is observed as compared with fibre necrosis and regeneration in active myositis.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
coreConcept: Jo-1 Antibody and ILD in DM
statement: A 48-year-old female presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from her bed. Examination reveals violaceous discoloration of the eyelids with periorbital edema and scaly, erythematous plaques over the distal interphalangeal joints. She also reports a dry cough and exertional dyspnea. Which laboratory finding would be most strongly associated with her pulmonary symptoms?
options: Anticentromere antibodies
Markedly elevated serum ferritin
Low titer Rheumatoid Factor
Anti-topoisomerase 1 (Scl70) antibodies
Antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies
correctOption: Antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies
optionExplanations: Anticentromere antibodies are biomarkers for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSScl) and CREST syndrome, which do not typically feature the heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules seen here.
Elevated ferritin is a characteristic of Adult-onset Still’s disease, which presents with intermittent fever and rash, but not the specific heliotrope rash of dermatomyositis.
While RF can be positive in various autoimmune diseases, it is not the marker of choice for dermatomyositis-associated interstitial lung disease.
Scl70 antibodies are associated with interstitial lung disease in systemic sclerosis (dcSScl), but this patient has dermatomyositis (heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules).

The patient presents with classic dermatomyositis and features of interstitial lung disease (ILD). In the context of inflammatory myopathies, Jo-1 antibodies are the specific marker associated with ILD.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1043 (Book Page) / 1428: Interstitial lung disease occurs in up to 30% of patients and is associated with the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies.

category: Define polymyositis and dermatomyositis, highlighting their autoimmune basis
statement: What is the primary role of pharmacological agents like Methotrexate and Azathioprine in the management of polymyositis?
options: They are the treatment of choice for pharyngeal muscle involvement.
They are specifically used to treat associated malignancy in paraneoplastic cases.
They are used as first-line induction agents to replace glucocorticoids entirely.
They target the IL-1 receptor to reduce acute phase reactants.
They serve as steroid-sparing agents for patients requiring long-term maintenance.
correctOption: They serve as steroid-sparing agents for patients requiring long-term maintenance.
optionExplanations: Pharyngeal involvement is an emergency often requiring high-dose IV methylprednisolone, not just oral steroid-sparing agents like MTX.
Malignancy-associated myositis requires treating the underlying cancer; MTX and Azathioprine are immunosuppressants for the myositis itself, not chemotherapeutic agents for the malignancy.
Glucocorticoids remain the first-line treatment for induction. Methotrexate is typically added as an adjunct or for those who do not respond fully.
